01.01.thesis: Start by naming the actors, operations, and promises. For a short link, creation and redirect are separate operations with different latency and correctness needs.
01.01.design: Write down ownership, retention, access rules, traffic, and what happens when a dependency fails before choosing infrastructure.
01.01.mechanics: Separate functional requirements from constraints: actors and operations describe what the product does, while latency, availability, retention, privacy, and recovery targets constrain its implementation. Record assumptions explicitly and assign an owner to resolve each one.
01.01.example: For a link shortener, list create, redirect, disable, and report operations. Specify whether links expire, how quickly disablement must take effect, which redirects are counted, and expected read/write volume.
01.01.failure: Vague words hide incompatible expectations. “Always available” conflicts with a strict dependency on a single analytics store; “fast” is meaningless without a percentile, region, and measurement point.
01.01.review: Which single missing product answer would force you to change the data model or synchronous request path?

01.02.thesis: Draw the path from request to durable state and back. Keep the diagram at the level of responsibilities until the data flow is clear.
01.02.design: Mark the source of truth, synchronous calls, and any background work; a box without a reason to exist can wait.
01.02.mechanics: A logical design identifies responsibilities and the information each one owns before selecting vendors or deployment units. Trace reads and writes end to end, mark synchronous boundaries, and name the authoritative record.
01.02.example: A shortener can start with an HTTP handler, a mapping repository, a relational database, and an optional cache. The redirect handler reads by code; creation writes a unique mapping; reporting consumes redirect events separately.
01.02.failure: A diagram that omits ownership creates duplicate sources of truth. Drawing microservices before identifying data ownership often commits the design to network calls and distributed transactions without a product reason.
01.02.review: Can you label every box with a responsibility and every arrow with the data and failure behavior it carries?

01.03.thesis: Turn “fast” and “reliable” into measurable targets, such as p99 latency, monthly availability, recovery time, and data loss tolerance.
01.03.design: Measure the user-visible operation, not only the health of one service.
01.03.mechanics: Non-functional requirements should be observable service-level indicators with a target and time window. Common measures include successful request ratio, p95 or p99 latency, freshness, recovery time, and tolerated data loss.
01.03.example: For redirects, define p99 server latency below a chosen threshold in each region and availability over a rolling month. For accepted link creation, define whether a successful response means the mapping has reached durable storage.
01.03.failure: A system may meet average latency while a small group of users sees very slow responses. Availability measured only by process health can also look green while requests fail at the database or edge.
01.03.review: What user-visible measurement would reveal that the system is unhealthy even while all processes report healthy?

01.04.thesis: Every design buys one property with another: latency with memory, isolation with coordination, or simplicity with limited scale.
01.04.design: State the workload and failure mode that justify each tradeoff, then record when the choice should be revisited.
01.04.mechanics: A design tradeoff is a choice between measurable properties under a stated workload. Compare options against the same requirements and include operational burden, not just latency or throughput.
01.04.example: For read-heavy redirects, caching can reduce database load and latency. It also adds stale data after a link is disabled, so the design must include cache expiry or explicit invalidation in the requirement.
01.04.failure: Tradeoffs become cargo cult when the workload is missing. A cache, replica, or service split may add cost and failure modes without moving the metric that actually matters.
01.04.review: Name the metric gained, the metric paid, and the evidence that would make you reverse this choice.

01.05.thesis: Availability is the ability to answer, durability is the survival of accepted data, consistency is agreement about its value, and cost limits every plan.
01.05.design: Specify the promise per operation; a read and a payment commit may need very different priorities.
01.05.mechanics: Availability is whether an operation can complete, durability is whether acknowledged data survives, and consistency describes which value a reader can observe. Cost includes the capacity and operations needed to provide each guarantee.
01.05.example: A redirect may be served from a replica that is seconds behind, while link creation waits for a durable primary commit. These are different guarantees for two operations in the same product.
01.05.failure: A successful write response is misleading if it can be lost on failover. A highly available read path may return old state, so revocation and balance-like operations need explicit freshness rules.
01.05.review: For each operation, what is the acceptable stale-read window and which failures may lose acknowledged data?

01.06.thesis: Convert daily volume to average and peak requests per second, then estimate bytes per record, replication, indexes, and retention.
01.06.design: Keep units visible. Add headroom for bursts, but do not turn rough assumptions into false precision.
01.06.mechanics: Capacity planning starts with rates and bytes: average requests per second, peak-to-average ratio, record size, index overhead, replication, and retention. Show assumptions and calculate a range instead of one precise-looking number.
01.06.example: One million new links per day is about 12 writes per second on average; redirects may be many times higher. Multiply retained rows by encoded row plus index size, then account for replicas and growth.
01.06.failure: Daily averages hide short bursts and hot tenants. Omitting indexes, metadata, and replicas underestimates storage; planning to theoretical maximum throughput leaves no room for maintenance or failures.
01.06.review: Which input has the largest uncertainty, and how much does doubling it change the capacity estimate?

01.07.thesis: A server can overlap I/O-bound requests with event loops or threads, while CPU work still needs cores or workers.
01.07.design: Set concurrency limits against memory and downstream capacity; unlimited in-flight requests become a queue inside the process.
01.07.mechanics: A server accepts connections, parses requests, performs CPU work, waits on I/O, and returns responses. Threads, event loops, and worker pools overlap waiting differently, but all share finite memory, file descriptors, CPU, and downstream capacity.
01.07.example: An event-loop server can keep many database-bound requests in flight while each awaits I/O. A CPU-heavy image transform may need a bounded worker pool or separate service so it does not stall unrelated requests.
01.07.failure: An unbounded number of in-flight operations turns overload into memory growth and longer queues. A blocked event loop, exhausted connection pool, or slow downstream can make every request wait together.
01.07.review: Where does each request wait, and what explicit limit stops that queue from consuming all available resources?

01.08.thesis: Vertical scaling increases one machine’s resources; horizontal scaling adds machines and forces shared-state decisions.
01.08.design: Scale the bottleneck shown by measurements, then plan for the point where one host becomes an availability risk.
01.08.mechanics: Vertical scaling makes one node larger; horizontal scaling adds nodes and requires state placement, load distribution, and failure handling. The useful comparison includes the next bottleneck after the first resource is relieved.
01.08.example: If database CPU is saturated but memory and storage are healthy, a larger database host may be the smallest next step. Stateless web handlers can often scale horizontally behind a load balancer once shared session state is externalized.
01.08.failure: One large host remains a failure domain and has an upper limit. More nodes can expose hot keys, distributed coordination, and uneven load; adding replicas does not fix a single writer bottleneck.
01.08.review: Which measured resource is saturated, and what new bottleneck appears after you add capacity to it?

01.09.thesis: A monolith keeps transactions and deployment simple; services offer independent ownership and scaling at the price of network failure.
01.09.design: Split along stable business boundaries when team and deployment pressure make that cost worthwhile.
01.09.mechanics: A monolith packages multiple domain capabilities into one deployable unit; microservices deploy capabilities independently across network boundaries. Service count is less important than ownership, change rate, and data boundaries.
01.09.example: A small catalog can keep product, pricing, and inventory modules in one process while enforcing clear module APIs. If inventory later needs independent scaling and team ownership, it can be extracted behind a versioned contract.
01.09.failure: A monolith with tangled modules makes every change risky, but splitting it creates network failure, deployment coordination, observability, and data consistency work. A remote call cannot provide a local transaction for free.
01.09.review: Can the team name an independent reason to deploy or scale this boundary and identify who owns its data?

01.10.thesis: A repository keeps domain code focused on operations such as save and find while hiding storage details.
01.10.design: Do not hide query shape or transaction boundaries so completely that callers cannot reason about cost and correctness.
01.10.mechanics: The repository pattern centralizes persistence operations behind domain-shaped methods. It can keep storage mechanics out of business rules, but its interface should still expose meaningful transaction and query behavior.
01.10.example: An OrderRepository might provide `createPending`, `findForCheckout`, and `markPaid` within a transaction rather than a generic `get` and `save`. The service layer then expresses checkout rules without SQL scattered through handlers.
01.10.failure: A generic repository can hide query count, locking, or pagination and encourage inefficient read-modify-write cycles. Abstractions that erase important database guarantees make correctness harder to review.
01.10.review: Does the interface make the needed transaction boundary and expected query cost visible to its caller?

01.11.thesis: Model stable identities and relationships first, then leave explicit extension points for fields that will change.
01.11.design: Validate extensions and version their meaning; an unbounded JSON column can become a schema nobody understands.
01.11.mechanics: Extensible data modeling allows known stable fields to evolve without turning every new attribute into a schema migration. Structured fields should remain typed and validated; extension data needs ownership, limits, and version semantics.
01.11.example: A product can keep price, seller, and availability as typed columns while storing partner-specific display attributes in a validated JSON object. Search-critical fields can be promoted into indexed columns when queries require them.
01.11.failure: An open-ended attributes bag accumulates inconsistent names, types, and meanings. Unknown fields can also become an injection, size, or privacy risk if accepted and indexed without controls.
01.11.review: Which fields are core invariants, and what validation and migration path applies to extensions?

01.12.thesis: Compare cost per successful operation at expected and peak load, including storage, transfer, replicas, and staff time.
01.12.design: Prefer a simpler component when its capacity margin is sufficient; unused resilience still has a bill.
01.12.mechanics: Cost-aware architecture compares cost per useful operation across compute, storage, network transfer, replicas, and engineering time. Reliability features also have a cost, so provision for a named failure and recovery target.
01.12.example: Estimate monthly cost for the expected peak, then compare a managed database with self-operated nodes including on-call effort and backup storage. Unit cost per thousand redirects can show whether cache work has meaningful payoff.
01.12.failure: Optimizing one bill line can increase total cost: aggressive compression consumes CPU, and cross-region replication increases transfer. A cheap system that cannot recover within the product’s target is not actually equivalent.
01.12.review: What cost metric reflects the product’s value, and which reliability target must remain fixed while you optimize it?

01.13.thesis: New infrastructure adds deployment, monitoring, recovery, and expertise obligations.
01.13.design: Use the smallest system that satisfies measured requirements; define the trigger that would justify adding the next component.
01.13.mechanics: Infrastructure is justified when a measured limit or required guarantee cannot be met by the current system. A new component also adds deploy, monitor, secure, upgrade, and restore work.
01.13.example: Keep a single relational database while its measured capacity and recovery behavior satisfy the brief. Add a cache only after read latency or database load crosses a threshold, then compare hit rate and invalidation cost.
01.13.failure: Premature queues, caches, and service splits create state that must be reconciled and failure modes nobody practices. Waiting too long can also fail; define a trigger and owner before a limit is reached.
01.13.review: What metric, trend, or incident would make you add this component, and how will you remove it if it does not help?

02.01.thesis: An API contract names resources or operations, input validation, errors, pagination, and compatibility rules.
02.01.design: Make retries and side effects explicit; clients need to know whether repeating a call is safe.
02.01.mechanics: An API contract specifies operation semantics, schemas, validation, authentication, error codes, pagination, idempotency, and compatibility. It is a promise to clients and must describe observable behavior, not only endpoint syntax.
02.01.example: For `POST /links`, define accepted URL formats, key ownership, conflict behavior, and whether a repeated idempotency key returns the first result. For listing, define stable sort and cursor behavior.
02.01.failure: Ambiguous errors lead clients to retry unsafe operations or parse message text. A breaking field rename can strand older clients that deploy on a different schedule.
02.01.review: Can an independent client implement success, retry, conflict, and pagination behavior using only the contract?

02.02.thesis: A remote call crosses a failure boundary even when both services run in one cluster.
02.02.design: Budget timeouts across the whole request, propagate context, and choose which failures can be handled asynchronously.
02.02.mechanics: Service-to-service communication can be synchronous request-response or asynchronous message delivery. Synchronous calls couple latency and availability; asynchronous calls require durable messages, acknowledgements, retries, and observable lag.
02.02.example: A checkout request can synchronously authorize payment but enqueue receipt email after the order commit. The response path should have a timeout budget shared across gateway, application, and payment provider.
02.02.failure: A dependency that hangs consumes connection slots and pushes latency upstream. Async work can be duplicated or delayed, so consumers need idempotency and operators need a way to inspect and replay failures.
02.02.review: Which work must finish before the caller can proceed, and what durable record exists for deferred work?

02.03.thesis: HTTP is the transport, REST is a resource-oriented style, and gRPC provides typed RPC contracts over HTTP/2.
02.03.design: Choose by client ecosystem, streaming needs, and evolution costs rather than treating one protocol as inherently faster.
02.03.mechanics: HTTP defines message transport and semantics; REST organizes APIs around resources and standard methods; gRPC uses generated typed contracts over HTTP/2. These are related choices, not competing synonyms.
02.03.example: Use HTTP JSON for a public browser-facing API where inspection and broad client support matter. A typed internal RPC may suit frequent service calls or streaming when all clients can manage generated schemas.
02.03.failure: Switching protocols does not repair a poor data contract. Binary RPC can complicate browser access and debugging; REST endpoints can still be chatty or inconsistent.
02.03.review: Who are the clients, what interaction pattern do they need, and how will the schema evolve without synchronized releases?

02.04.thesis: TCP preserves ordered reliable bytes; UDP leaves delivery and ordering to the application and can reduce handshake overhead.
02.04.design: Use UDP when the application can tolerate or repair loss, as in real-time media; use TCP for ordinary business requests.
02.04.mechanics: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream and retransmits lost data; UDP sends datagrams without those guarantees. Reliability and congestion behavior can be added above UDP, but then the application owns them.
02.04.example: A file upload typically benefits from TCP delivery and congestion control. Real-time voice may prefer timely newer packets over retransmitting a late audio frame, with codecs and jitter buffers repairing limited loss.
02.04.failure: TCP head-of-line blocking can delay later bytes behind a missing segment. UDP can lose, reorder, or duplicate datagrams, and ignoring congestion control can harm both the application and network.
02.04.review: Is freshness more valuable than complete ordered delivery, and which layer detects loss or limits sending rate?

02.05.thesis: A gateway enforces cross-cutting API policies, while a load balancer distributes traffic among healthy backends.
02.05.design: Place authentication and quotas at the correct trust boundary; avoid duplicating policy across layers.
02.05.mechanics: An API gateway is a policy and routing boundary for client APIs; a load balancer selects a healthy backend instance. They may share a product label but solve different problems.
02.05.example: A gateway can authenticate a mobile token, apply per-customer quotas, and route `/orders` to an order service. A load balancer behind it can distribute those requests across healthy order instances.
02.05.failure: Putting all policy in a load balancer may leave no place for client identity or API versioning. A gateway can become a bottleneck or single control point if every request depends on it.
02.05.review: Which decision needs application identity and policy, and which decision only needs healthy capacity selection?

02.06.thesis: A load balancer selects healthy targets with round robin, least connections, or a workload-aware policy.
02.06.design: Health checks should test readiness, and draining should let in-flight requests finish before removing a target.
02.06.mechanics: A load balancer distributes requests using algorithms such as round robin, least active requests, or weighted routing. Health checks and connection draining matter as much as the selection algorithm.
02.06.example: For stateless HTTP handlers, send traffic only to instances that pass a readiness check, and stop new requests before deployment while allowing existing requests to finish.
02.06.failure: A process can answer a shallow health endpoint while its database pool is unusable. Sticky routing can overload one host, and aggressive health checks can eject all nodes during a shared dependency slowdown.
02.06.review: Does readiness represent the ability to serve real work, and can targets be removed without dropping in-flight requests?

02.07.thesis: Consistent hashing keeps related keys on a stable subset of servers when membership changes.
02.07.design: Virtual nodes smooth uneven distribution, but hot keys still need a separate mitigation.
02.07.mechanics: Consistent hashing maps keys and servers onto a ring so membership changes move only a fraction of keys. Virtual nodes smooth placement; replicas provide alternate owners.
02.07.example: Route a user’s cached session key to one of many cache nodes. When one node is added, most keys keep their prior owner, avoiding a full cache cold start.
02.07.failure: Hash balance does not imply traffic balance: one celebrity key can dominate its node. Membership disagreement can send the same key to inconsistent owners, so ring versions must be coordinated.
02.07.review: How are node membership changes published, and what happens when one key is far hotter than the rest?

02.08.thesis: An event contract defines identity, schema, occurrence time, producer, and version—not just a payload name.
02.08.design: Consumers must tolerate duplicates and compatible schema evolution because events may outlive the producer’s deployment.
02.08.mechanics: An event contract gives an event a stable name, unique ID, producer, occurrence time, schema version, and meaning. Events describe facts that happened; commands request work to happen.
02.08.example: `OrderPaid` can include order ID, payment reference, amount, currency, and event version. A receipt consumer and analytics consumer can interpret the same fact independently.
02.08.failure: Renaming a field or changing a unit silently corrupts consumers. Delivery may be duplicated, and schema changes roll out across independently deployed producers and readers.
02.08.review: Could a consumer safely process this event twice, and can it distinguish a compatible schema change from a changed meaning?

02.09.thesis: Set a bounded timeout, retry only recoverable failures, and use an idempotency key for side-effecting requests.
02.09.design: Persist the result against the key so a retry after a lost response does not repeat the effect.
02.09.mechanics: Timeouts bound waiting; retries recover transient failures; idempotency makes repeating a side-effecting operation safe. The retry policy should cap attempts and use backoff with jitter.
02.09.example: A client submits a payment intent with one stable key. The server stores the key and final response with the operation, so a retry after a lost response returns the same result rather than charging again.
02.09.failure: Retrying every error can amplify an outage. A retry after the server committed but before the response arrived is the dangerous case; a key stored only in process memory does not protect across restart.
02.09.review: What is the retryable failure set, maximum retry budget, and durable lookup that proves a request already happened?

02.10.thesis: Batching amortizes network and storage overhead across multiple items.
02.10.design: Bound both batch size and wait time; a large batch can improve throughput while making individual requests slower.
02.10.mechanics: Batching reduces per-operation overhead by grouping work, but adds waiting, memory, and failure coupling. A batch needs limits on item count, bytes, and flush time.
02.10.example: A metrics collector can send up to a fixed number of events or flush after a short interval, whichever comes first. The receiver can acknowledge a batch while reporting individual malformed records.
02.10.failure: A large batch can exceed transport limits or make one invalid item reject all valid work. Waiting to fill a batch increases latency under light traffic.
02.10.review: What is the maximum acceptable added delay, and can a partial batch failure be retried without duplicating accepted items?

02.11.thesis: Backpressure tells producers when consumers cannot keep up.
02.11.design: Use bounded queues, credits, or rejection; an unbounded buffer merely postpones overload until memory runs out.
02.11.mechanics: Backpressure communicates downstream capacity to upstream producers through bounded queues, credits, or explicit rejection. It keeps overload visible and prevents queue growth from consuming all memory.
02.11.example: A worker pool can accept only a fixed number of pending image jobs. When full, the API returns a retryable response or stores work in a durable queue with a quota.
02.11.failure: An unbounded queue hides overload until the oldest job is stale or the process runs out of memory. Dropping work silently makes the queue look healthy while user intent disappears.
02.11.review: Where is the first bounded buffer, and what exact response or pause does the producer see when it fills?

02.12.thesis: The slowest requests shape p99 latency and user experience even when the mean looks healthy.
02.12.design: Measure each dependency and queue separately; a fanout request amplifies the chance of encountering a slow tail.
02.12.mechanics: Tail latency describes slow percentiles, which can dominate a user request even when the mean is low. Fanout multiplies this effect because the overall response waits for one or more slow dependencies.
02.12.example: If a page fetches 20 services in parallel and each has a 1% chance of exceeding a threshold, the chance at least one is slow is much higher than 1%. Hedging or partial responses can reduce the effect at added cost.
02.12.failure: Averages conceal saturation and queue buildup. Hedged requests can double traffic during the worst moment unless they are cancelled and tightly bounded.
02.12.review: Which percentile and deadline matter to the caller, and can the response succeed with a missing or stale component?

02.13.thesis: Load shedding refuses lower-priority work before overload collapses every request.
02.13.design: Choose priorities and an explicit response, and keep the admission decision ahead of expensive work.
02.13.mechanics: Load shedding rejects work before the system exhausts CPU, memory, connections, or queue capacity. Admission decisions should account for priority and the cost of each request.
02.13.example: During overload, preserve checkout confirmation and reject expensive recommendation refreshes with a retry-after hint. Use concurrency limits or a token bucket at the edge of the constrained resource.
02.13.failure: Dropping arbitrary requests can discard writes or starve low-volume tenants. If shedding occurs after expensive parsing or database work, it protects too little.
02.13.review: Which work is safe to defer or reject, and where can it be refused before consuming scarce capacity?

03.01.thesis: Start relational design with entities, keys, cardinality, and invariants enforced by constraints.
03.01.design: Normalize for correctness, then denormalize only for a measured read pattern with a clear update path.
03.01.mechanics: Relational design represents entities and relationships with keys, constraints, and transactions. Normalize duplicated facts to protect updates, then add derived or denormalized views for measured access patterns.
03.01.example: A commerce model can hold customers, orders, order lines, products, and payments in separate tables. Foreign keys protect relationships; a transaction ensures the order and its lines appear together.
03.01.failure: Missing constraints allow invalid states that every application path must remember to reject. Over-normalized hot reads can require costly joins, while careless denormalization creates conflicting copies.
03.01.review: Which invariant can the database enforce directly, and which read path justifies keeping a derived copy?

03.02.thesis: A SQL-backed key-value store needs a unique key, value representation, version or timestamp, and clear overwrite semantics.
03.02.design: Index the lookup key and decide whether writes are insert-only, conditional, or last-write-wins.
03.02.mechanics: A SQL-backed key-value table needs a primary key, a value encoding, optional expiry, and explicit write semantics. A unique constraint prevents two concurrent writers from claiming the same key.
03.02.example: Store configuration by `(tenant_id, key)` with a JSON value and version. Use conditional update on the version when callers must avoid overwriting a newer value.
03.02.failure: A schema that supports only primary-key lookup may disappoint once secondary queries appear. Unbounded values and missing tenant scoping can turn a simple table into a costly security boundary.
03.02.review: Are reads always by key, and how should concurrent create, overwrite, delete, and expiry behave?

03.03.thesis: An index trades write and storage cost for a faster access path.
03.03.design: Index predicates and sort order used by real queries; check plans rather than indexing every column.
03.03.mechanics: An index is an ordered or hashed structure maintained with table writes to accelerate selected lookups. It adds storage and write work, so index design follows predicates, joins, ordering, and selectivity.
03.03.example: For `WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC`, a composite index on `(tenant_id, created_at)` can support both filtering and ordering. A covering index may avoid fetching full rows.
03.03.failure: An index on a low-selectivity field may not help; too many indexes slow inserts and consume cache. An index order that mismatches the query may still scan many entries.
03.03.review: Which exact query shape should become cheaper, and what write cost and storage do you accept for that index?

03.04.thesis: A B-tree keeps sorted keys in pages, supporting point lookups and ranges with logarithmic navigation.
03.04.design: Page locality and key order matter; a random write pattern may cost more than a sequential one.
03.04.mechanics: A B-tree stores sorted keys in pages and keeps internal nodes as separators, letting the engine find a leaf with a small number of page reads. Leaves can support ordered traversal and range scans.
03.04.example: A database can find account ID 812 by descending separator pages, then scan adjacent leaf entries for accounts in a range. Page splits preserve order when an insertion fills a leaf.
03.04.failure: Random inserts may trigger splits and write amplification; a hot root or poor cache behavior can limit performance. A range query over many matches still has to read those matching rows.
03.04.review: Does the workload need point lookup, ordered range scan, or both, and how selective is the range?

03.05.thesis: A planner estimates row counts and chooses scans, joins, and indexes.
03.05.design: Compare estimated with actual rows using EXPLAIN ANALYZE; stale statistics often explain surprising plans.
03.05.mechanics: A query planner compares possible access paths using statistics about row counts, value distributions, and costs. The chosen plan may change as data grows or statistics become stale.
03.05.example: Use an execution plan to see whether a filtered join uses the intended index, how many rows each stage actually processes, and where sort or hash work spills to disk.
03.05.failure: A plan can look cheap from inaccurate estimates and become disastrous at production cardinality. Adding an index without checking the plan may leave the original scan untouched.
03.05.review: Where do estimated and actual row counts diverge, and which stage dominates elapsed time and I/O?

03.06.thesis: Locks and isolation decide what concurrent transactions may observe or modify.
03.06.design: Keep transactions short and test conflicting writes; isolation names alone do not prove an application invariant.
03.06.mechanics: Locks prevent conflicting changes; isolation levels determine which concurrent reads and writes can observe each other. Correctness depends on the invariant and database-specific semantics, not only the isolation label.
03.06.example: To reserve the final seat, lock the inventory row or use a conditional decrement where remaining quantity is positive. Commit the reservation and related order state in one short transaction.
03.06.failure: Long transactions hold locks and block unrelated work. A check-then-write sequence outside one transaction can oversell; deadlocks require safe retry of the entire idempotent transaction.
03.06.review: What concurrent interleaving breaks the invariant, and which lock or constraint prevents that interleaving?

03.07.thesis: MVCC lets readers see a stable snapshot while writers create newer row versions.
03.07.design: Old versions need cleanup, and long-running transactions can prevent that cleanup from advancing.
03.07.mechanics: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so a transaction reads a consistent snapshot while writers create newer versions. Readers often avoid blocking writers, but old versions remain until no active snapshot needs them.
03.07.example: A report started at time T can continue to see the row values valid at T while checkout updates current inventory. New transactions see the committed newer version.
03.07.failure: A long-running snapshot can retain dead tuples and grow storage or slow cleanup. Applications may mistake snapshot isolation for serializable behavior and still permit write skew.
03.07.review: What is the transaction’s snapshot boundary, and can concurrent transactions each pass a check while jointly violating a rule?

03.08.thesis: A write-ahead log records changes before data pages are flushed so committed work can be replayed after a crash.
03.08.design: Check the durability settings and recovery path; a successful API response should have a defined persistence point.
03.08.mechanics: A write-ahead log records changes before the database flushes affected data pages. Recovery replays committed records after a crash and discards incomplete transactions according to the engine’s rules.
03.08.example: On commit, the database can flush the transaction’s log record; the table page may reach disk later. After power loss, redo reconstructs the acknowledged row from the log.
03.08.failure: If commit acknowledgement does not wait for the required log durability, a crash can lose a “successful” write. Broken log archival also prevents point-in-time recovery even when snapshots exist.
03.08.review: What exact durability point does commit acknowledge, and do archived logs cover the required recovery window?

03.09.thesis: A ticket server allocates ranges of identifiers to writers to avoid a centralized call per row.
03.09.design: Range leasing improves throughput but leaves gaps on crashes; use it only if gaps are acceptable.
03.09.mechanics: A ticket server allocates blocks of IDs to clients so each insert does not need a global sequence round trip. It exchanges centralized coordination for range leases and gaps.
03.09.example: A worker requests 1,000 IDs, persists the range locally, and allocates from it until exhausted. After a restart, unused values may be skipped while the next lease begins above the old range.
03.09.failure: If two ticket servers allocate overlapping ranges after failover, uniqueness breaks. If one server is a bottleneck, range sizing and refill frequency determine whether the design helps.
03.09.review: Can IDs contain gaps, and what durable coordination prevents a restarted allocator from reissuing a leased range?

03.10.thesis: Scale SQL by improving queries and indexes, then add replicas or partitioning where the measured bottleneck demands it.
03.10.design: Replicas make reads stale, and sharding complicates joins and transactions; quantify the benefit first.
03.10.mechanics: Relational scaling progresses from query and schema tuning to read replicas, partitioning, and sharding. Each step adds consistency or transaction constraints, so move only after identifying the limiting resource.
03.10.example: Route analytical reads to a replica if seconds of lag are acceptable; keep a user’s read-after-write path on the primary or wait until its replication position catches up.
03.10.failure: Replicas do not increase write capacity and can return stale results. Sharding complicates global uniqueness, joins, transactions, and rebalancing.
03.10.review: Is the bottleneck reads, writes, storage, or a single hot table, and which application guarantees change with the proposed scale step?

03.11.thesis: Online index creation reduces blocking while a table remains in use.
03.11.design: Budget extra disk and I/O, monitor progress, and keep a rollback plan for a slow or failed build.
03.11.mechanics: Online index builds keep normal reads and writes available by scanning existing rows while tracking concurrent changes. Exact locking and failure behavior depend on the database engine.
03.11.example: Build an index concurrently on a large live table, monitor progress and disk use, then confirm it is valid before deploying a query that depends on it.
03.11.failure: The build competes for I/O and can leave an invalid index after failure. DDL may still take brief locks, so deploy tooling needs a timeout and an operator-visible rollback.
03.11.review: How much extra disk and I/O will the build need, and how will you detect an invalid or unfinished index?

03.12.thesis: Use expand, migrate, contract: add compatible fields, backfill, switch readers and writers, then remove old fields.
03.12.design: Deployments overlap, so both schema versions must work during the transition.
03.12.mechanics: Schema evolution must support old and new application versions during rollout. Expand-and-contract adds compatible fields, backfills, switches reads and writes, then removes obsolete structure later.
03.12.example: Add a nullable `display_name` field, deploy code that writes both old and new representations, backfill existing rows, switch reads, then remove the old field only after all consumers upgrade.
03.12.failure: A destructive rename can break a rolling deployment. A backfill without checkpoints can overload the database or repeat inconsistently after interruption.
03.12.review: Can the current and previous application versions both operate safely at every migration step?

03.13.thesis: Soft deletion records a removal state while retaining rows for recovery or audit.
03.13.design: Apply the predicate consistently to reads, uniqueness rules, and eventual purge jobs.
03.13.mechanics: Soft delete marks a record as removed while keeping its data for recovery, audit, or a retention period. It changes read visibility and uniqueness semantics across the whole application.
03.13.example: Add `deleted_at`, exclude deleted rows from ordinary queries, and use a partial unique index so a user may recreate a name after the original is removed if product rules permit it.
03.13.failure: One query that forgets the deletion predicate can expose removed data. Retained rows still need a purge schedule if law or product policy requires final erasure.
03.13.review: Which readers must hide the record, how does uniqueness work after deletion, and when is irreversible purge allowed?

04.01.thesis: Choose a non-relational store for an access pattern or scale property it actually serves, not for a vague promise of flexibility.
04.01.design: Write down required queries, transaction boundaries, and consistency before selecting a data model.
04.01.mechanics: NoSQL is a family of storage models with different query, consistency, and scaling behavior, not one design style. Select a store from required access patterns and invariants.
04.01.example: If an application fetches a whole user profile by ID and updates nested preferences together, a document store may fit. If it needs arbitrary reporting joins and multi-row constraints, relational storage may be simpler.
04.01.failure: Picking a store from a throughput slogan ignores secondary indexes, transaction scope, operational skill, and migration cost. A later query pattern can force expensive duplication.
04.01.review: List the top reads and writes, their consistency needs, and the invariant that must survive concurrent updates before selecting the model.

04.02.thesis: Document stores group related fields into one retrievable object; key-value stores excel when the key is known.
04.02.design: Large mutable documents and secondary queries change the cost profile; model the update path as well as the read.
04.02.mechanics: Document stores group related values into a record; key-value stores retrieve opaque values by exact key. Their distinction is how much the engine understands and indexes inside the value.
04.02.example: A profile document can be fetched and replaced as one unit when its size is bounded and fields change together. A session cache can use an opaque serialized value when no field-level query is needed.
04.02.failure: Large documents increase write amplification and contention when one small field changes. Treating an opaque value as queryable data leads to application scans and accidental schema lock-in.
04.02.review: Do callers need predicates on fields inside the value, or is exact-key retrieval enough?

04.03.thesis: Columnar storage groups values by column for analytic scans; wide-column stores partition rows by key for operational access.
04.03.design: Their similar names hide different workloads, so start with query shape and update frequency.
04.03.mechanics: Columnar analytics engines store values by column to scan a subset of fields across many rows; wide-column operational stores organize rows by partition key and clustered columns.
04.03.example: An analytics query summing one metric over months benefits from reading that column only. A device event store may partition by device and time to fetch a device’s recent events.
04.03.failure: Columnar storage can be poor for frequent point updates; wide-column schemas are query-first and may duplicate data for each access path. Similar terminology can conceal different engines.
04.03.review: Is the dominant work a broad scan over a few fields or targeted operational reads by partition key?

04.04.thesis: A graph database is useful when relationship traversal is the main operation and depth is not known in advance.
04.04.design: For shallow, fixed joins, relational indexes may be simpler and faster to operate.
04.04.mechanics: Graph stores optimize traversal across relationships represented as edges. Their value increases when queries follow variable-depth paths or relationship neighborhoods.
04.04.example: To find friends-of-friends with shared attributes, begin at a user node and traverse follow edges while filtering candidates. Keep edge direction and relationship properties explicit.
04.04.failure: A graph engine may add operational cost for simple fixed joins. High-degree nodes and unrestricted traversals can expand candidate sets dramatically.
04.04.review: How many relationship hops are queried, how predictable is the traversal, and what is the worst-case neighborhood size?

04.05.thesis: Partitioning divides data or work by a key so one node does not own everything.
04.05.design: Pick a key that distributes load and supports common queries; cross-partition operations become more expensive.
04.05.mechanics: Partitioning assigns records to smaller ownership ranges using a partition key. The key controls both distribution and which queries can be served without fanout.
04.05.example: Partition orders by customer ID when most requests load one customer’s history. Store the customer key with every record and paginate within that partition.
04.05.failure: A key that concentrates popular tenants produces a hot shard. Queries without the key scatter across partitions, and cross-shard writes may lose atomicity.
04.05.review: Which query includes the partition key, and what distribution does the key produce at the busiest tenant?

04.06.thesis: A hot partition appears when one key or range receives disproportionate traffic.
04.06.design: Measure per-key load; salting, write spreading, or isolating a celebrity key can restore balance.
04.06.mechanics: A hot partition receives far more requests or bytes than peers, so adding average capacity does not fix the overloaded owner. Detect skew using per-partition metrics.
04.06.example: If one product drives a sale, split writes across salted subkeys and merge them for reads, or isolate that product on dedicated capacity. For counters, shard increments and aggregate later.
04.06.failure: Salting adds read fanout and can make updates harder to deduplicate. Moving a hot key can create churn unless placement and routing change together.
04.06.review: How much of total traffic comes from the hottest key, and what read or write amplification will your mitigation add?

04.07.thesis: Hash keys onto a ring so adding a node remaps only part of the keyspace.
04.07.design: Replicas and virtual nodes improve balance, but placement changes still need controlled migration.
04.07.mechanics: Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping when nodes enter or leave a ring. Virtual nodes improve balance; replication places each key on several successors.
04.07.example: A cache client hashes a key to its first node and keeps using that node until membership changes. With replicas, reads may try another owner if one is unavailable.
04.07.failure: Ring updates that arrive at different times can split ownership and lose cache coherence. Hashing smooths key counts, not bytes or requests per key.
04.07.review: How are ring versions distributed consistently, and what mechanism handles a single hot key that hashing cannot split?

04.08.thesis: Distributed IDs can use random values, leased ranges, or time plus worker and sequence bits.
04.08.design: Decide whether order, compactness, predictability, and offline generation matter before choosing a scheme.
04.08.mechanics: Distributed ID generation must satisfy uniqueness under parallel creation and the product’s needs for ordering, size, and opacity. Options include random IDs, allocated ranges, or timestamp-and-worker layouts.
04.08.example: For a public resource identifier, a random UUID avoids a central allocator and is hard to enumerate. A time-ordered internal ID can improve index locality but may reveal creation order.
04.08.failure: Random IDs can fragment ordered indexes; timestamp schemes risk clock rollback or worker-ID collision. Monotonic IDs may leak volume and allow guessing.
04.08.review: Which requirement is essential—global uniqueness, approximate time order, compactness, or secrecy—and which can be relaxed?

04.09.thesis: UUIDs favor decentralized uniqueness, ObjectIds embed time and process information, and Snowflake-style IDs use sortable time bits.
04.09.design: Ordering is only approximate when clocks drift; do not use an ID as proof of causality.
04.09.mechanics: UUIDs provide a standardized large random or time-based identifier space; MongoDB ObjectIds combine timestamp and process data; Snowflake IDs pack time, worker, and sequence bits.
04.09.example: A public API can expose UUIDs while an internal event pipeline uses time-sortable IDs for efficient scans. Keep database primary-key requirements separate from public URL design.
04.09.failure: Time-bearing IDs leak approximate creation time. Worker or process collisions in structured IDs can create duplicates, while randomly distributed UUIDs can hurt B-tree locality.
04.09.review: Does the identifier need to be guess-resistant and sortable, and what clock or worker assumptions does the format make?

04.10.thesis: A Snowflake ID packs timestamp, worker ID, and per-time-unit sequence into one integer.
04.10.design: Handle clock rollback and sequence exhaustion explicitly, or duplicate and out-of-order IDs become possible.
04.10.mechanics: A Snowflake-style ID allocates bits to elapsed time, worker identity, and sequence within one time unit. Bit allocation sets the lifetime, machine count, and peak IDs per worker.
04.10.example: With a millisecond time field, each worker can issue sequence values until that millisecond changes. On sequence exhaustion it must wait or fail rather than repeat an ID.
04.10.failure: Clock rollback can make generated IDs move backward; reusing a worker ID during overlap creates collisions. Bit widths are long-lived compatibility decisions.
04.10.review: Calculate the maximum workers and IDs per time unit needed at peak, then define behavior for clock rollback and sequence exhaustion.

04.11.thesis: Clock skew can move a generated timestamp backward even while events continue forward.
04.11.design: Use logical sequence or database order for correctness; treat wall-clock order as an estimate.
04.11.mechanics: Wall clocks are imperfect and can jump or drift across hosts, so timestamp-sorted IDs do not establish causal order. Logical clocks or storage-assigned sequence numbers provide stronger ordering for specific scopes.
04.11.example: Two services may create IDs with timestamps 20 milliseconds apart in the wrong order because their clocks differ. A per-conversation sequence from the authoritative writer can still order messages correctly.
04.11.failure: Sorting distributed events only by timestamp can reorder a payment and its follow-up event. NTP corrections or VM pauses can move a generator’s clock backward.
04.11.review: What order does the application truly require—global, per key, or causal—and which system is authoritative for that order?

04.12.thesis: Keyset pagination resumes after the last sort key instead of skipping an ever-growing offset.
04.12.design: Use a unique tie-breaker and preserve the filter and sort order in the cursor.
04.12.mechanics: Keyset pagination uses the last seen sort key as a cursor, so later pages seek forward instead of skipping an increasing offset. A unique tie-breaker makes ordering total.
04.12.example: For posts sorted by `(created_at DESC, id DESC)`, return the next page where that tuple is less than the cursor tuple. Encode both values in an opaque cursor tied to the same filters.
04.12.failure: Using only a non-unique timestamp can duplicate or omit rows at page boundaries. Mutable sort fields can move records between pages; offset pagination also becomes expensive at deep offsets.
04.12.review: Is the sort order unique and stable, and what happens when new rows are inserted while a reader is paging?

04.13.thesis: A Bloom filter can prove absence but only suggest presence.
04.13.design: Size it for expected items and false-positive rate; still check the source of truth after a positive answer.
04.13.mechanics: A Bloom filter hashes each inserted key into a bit array. A zero bit proves absence; all set bits mean “possibly present,” with false positives controlled by memory and hash count.
04.13.example: Before reading an SSTable, test whether its filter might contain the target key. A negative skips disk I/O; a positive proceeds to the index and still verifies the actual record.
04.13.failure: A filter cannot safely authorize access or claim an item exists. Poor sizing raises false positives and wastes memory; rebuilding after data compaction must match the file contents.
04.13.review: What false-positive rate is acceptable, and does every positive result still consult the authoritative structure?

04.14.thesis: Keep frequently accessed data on a fast path and archive older data to cheaper storage.
04.14.design: Define retrieval time and retention promises before moving records out of the primary store.
04.14.mechanics: Hot storage optimizes recent and frequent access, while cold tiers reduce storage cost for older, rarely read records. Lifecycle transitions should preserve identity and retrieval semantics.
04.14.example: Keep the last month of telemetry in a queryable database, compact older data into partitioned object files, and retain a catalog so a historical request can locate the right object.
04.14.failure: Moving data before it is safely copied risks loss; a catalog that points to missing objects breaks retrieval. Cold access has higher latency and may require a restore step.
04.14.review: What are the retrieval-time promise and restore cost for each age tier, and how is a move verified before deleting the old copy?

05.01.thesis: Caches can sit in a browser, CDN, service process, or distributed store; each has a different scope and invalidation problem.
05.01.design: Name the authoritative store and the maximum acceptable staleness for each cached value.
05.01.mechanics: A cache is a copy optimized for a known access pattern. Browser, CDN, process-local, and distributed caches differ in scope, eviction, invalidation, and failure domain.
05.01.example: A product page can be cached at the edge for anonymous readers, while a user-specific cart stays in a private service cache. Use separate keys and freshness rules for data with different privacy or update behavior.
05.01.failure: A cache is not a source of truth. Mixing user identity into an incomplete key can leak data, while an unbounded local cache multiplies memory use across every application replica.
05.01.review: For each cached value, state its authority, key dimensions, maximum staleness, and behavior on miss.

05.02.thesis: A distributed cache shares hot data across service instances and can reduce database read load.
05.02.design: Partition keys, set memory limits, and plan for eviction or a full cache outage.
05.02.mechanics: A distributed cache spreads key ownership across nodes and often replicates hot values. Its capacity and availability depend on partitioning, eviction, network behavior, and client routing.
05.02.example: Use a cache cluster for frequently read product metadata with a TTL and a stable key scheme. Route keys consistently, cap object size, and measure hit rate by workload rather than only globally.
05.02.failure: Losing the cluster may send a sudden read surge to the database. Replicas can hold stale copies, and large keys can cause memory pressure even when request rate is modest.
05.02.review: Can the backing database absorb a cache-wide cold start, and what admission limit protects it if it cannot?

05.03.thesis: LRU favors recently used keys, LFU favors frequent keys, and size-aware policies protect memory better when objects vary.
05.03.design: Compare hit rate under real traffic; an algorithm name is not a substitute for workload measurement.
05.03.mechanics: LRU evicts the least recently accessed item; LFU evicts items used least often; FIFO ignores recency and frequency. Policies trade bookkeeping and scan resistance against memory efficiency.
05.03.example: For a workload with a small set of repeatedly read product records, LFU may retain useful keys through a one-time scan. For session data with changing recency, LRU may track current demand better.
05.03.failure: A scan can evict the hot working set under a naive LRU policy. LFU can retain yesterday’s popular keys too long unless it ages frequency; variable-size entries make object count a poor capacity measure.
05.03.review: What does “useful” mean for this workload—recent, frequent, or high value—and how does the policy respond to a traffic shift?

05.04.thesis: TTL bounds how long stale entries survive without explicit invalidation.
05.04.design: Add jitter to large groups of expirations, and remember that a reaper may delete later than the logical expiry.
05.04.mechanics: TTL sets a maximum logical age for a cache entry; physical reclamation may happen lazily on access or through background expiry work. Expiry and invalidation are separate mechanisms.
05.04.example: For catalog text, a several-minute TTL may bound staleness adequately. Add random jitter so millions of keys written together do not all expire at one instant.
05.04.failure: A TTL does not guarantee deletion at the exact deadline, and synchronized expiry can create a cache stampede. Too-long TTLs make revocation slow; too-short TTLs waste backend capacity.
05.04.review: What staleness is acceptable, and how do expiration jitter and refresh coalescing control a burst of misses?

05.05.thesis: When many requests miss the same key, one should load it while others wait or use stale data.
05.05.design: Bound the wait and cache negative results carefully to avoid turning one miss into a database stampede.
05.05.mechanics: Cache concurrency control prevents many simultaneous misses or writes from stampeding the backing store. Common tools include single-flight request coalescing, compare-and-set, and short leases.
05.05.example: When a popular key expires, let one caller fetch the value while other callers await that result or receive a permitted stale value. For writes, compare versions so an older fill cannot overwrite newer data.
05.05.failure: A lock with an unbounded wait turns the cache into a new queue. A delayed fill may arrive after an update and repopulate stale data unless versions or invalidation ordering are enforced.
05.05.review: How many backend loads can one missing key trigger, and can a delayed response overwrite a newer cached version?

05.06.thesis: A cache outage should have a deliberate fallback policy, not an accidental flood to the database.
05.06.design: Use admission limits or serve stale values when allowed; measure fallback capacity in advance.
05.06.mechanics: A cache outage needs a chosen fallback: read through to the database, serve stale data, reject lower-priority reads, or use another tier. Fallback capacity is part of the design.
05.06.example: If the cache fails, allow bounded direct reads for account pages while serving stale public catalog data from a secondary layer. Apply per-service concurrency limits to avoid a database surge.
05.06.failure: Failing open to the database can turn a small cache incident into a database outage. Failing closed can make safe reads unavailable. The policy should vary by data freshness and criticality.
05.06.review: Which values may be stale, which must be fresh, and how many fallback reads can the database sustain?

06.01.thesis: Distributed nodes communicate through a network that can delay, duplicate, reorder, or lose messages.
06.01.design: Describe the fault model before promising coordination; a timeout only proves that no answer arrived in time.
06.01.mechanics: A distributed system consists of independent nodes that communicate through a network with uncertain delay and partial failure. One component can be unreachable while others continue operating.
06.01.example: If an application server times out calling the database, it cannot know whether the request never arrived or committed and only the reply was lost. Request IDs and durable outcomes distinguish these cases.
06.01.failure: A timeout is not proof of failure; restarting or retrying can duplicate a side effect. A network partition can split membership views without either side seeing the full system.
06.01.review: For each remote operation, what outcomes are ambiguous after timeout and how does the caller resolve them safely?

06.02.thesis: Strong consistency makes newer writes visible according to a defined order; eventual consistency permits temporary divergence.
06.02.design: Pick the model per operation and state what a client may observe after its own write.
06.02.mechanics: Consistency models specify how operations appear across replicas. Linearizability gives a real-time order, sequential consistency gives one global order, and eventual consistency permits convergence after writes stop.
06.02.example: A profile preference can tolerate eventual propagation across regions, while a seat reservation needs a single agreed winner before confirmation. Reads can route based on the user’s required freshness.
06.02.failure: Using a stale replica for read-after-write can make a user believe their update vanished. “Eventual” without a convergence bound leaves clients unable to know when to retry or refresh.
06.02.review: What values may a client see immediately after its own write, and is there a maximum convergence time?

06.03.thesis: Replication copies data for availability or read capacity, but replicas can lag or disagree.
06.03.design: Define acknowledgement quorum, failover rules, and repair of divergent copies.
06.03.mechanics: Replication copies data to additional nodes for availability, locality, or read throughput. Synchronous acknowledgements reduce acknowledged data loss but add latency; asynchronous copies can lag.
06.03.example: A leader can commit an order and replicate it to followers. A read can use a nearby follower only if its staleness window is acceptable or the follower has applied the caller’s write position.
06.03.failure: Failover to a lagging replica may lose acknowledged writes or expose conflicting histories. Replica count alone does not help if every copy shares a rack or region failure.
06.03.review: Which independent failures must the data survive, and what replication position is required before success is acknowledged?

06.04.thesis: CAP describes the choice during a partition; PACELC adds latency versus consistency while the network is healthy.
06.04.design: Tie the theorem to a concrete read or write path instead of labeling an entire product with two letters.
06.04.mechanics: CAP concerns the choice between consistency and availability when messages between groups are partitioned. PACELC also frames the healthy-network choice between latency and consistency.
06.04.example: A globally distributed cart may accept region-local writes during a partition and reconcile later, while account balance updates may wait for a quorum to prevent conflicting debits.
06.04.failure: “Choose two” oversimplifies operations and failure modes. A system can be available for cached reads and unavailable for writes; labeling the whole database CP or AP hides that distinction.
06.04.review: During a partition, which operation continues, which one waits, and what conflict or staleness can users observe?

06.05.thesis: Physical clocks estimate time; logical clocks capture order or causality without trusting synchronized wall time.
06.05.design: Use a sequence, version, or Lamport clock when the application needs ordering guarantees.
06.05.mechanics: Physical clocks approximate time and may drift; Lamport clocks order causally related events, and vector clocks can reveal concurrent histories. Each captures a different notion of order.
06.05.example: A service increments a Lamport counter on each local event and raises it when receiving a larger remote value. This can order a distributed log without claiming that timestamps reflect exact wall time.
06.05.failure: Wall-clock sorting can reverse causally related events, while vector clocks grow with participants and need conflict handling. A timestamp is not a total order unless ties and skew are handled.
06.05.review: Does the application need elapsed time, total order, or causal order, and which clock model provides only that guarantee?

06.06.thesis: Consensus lets a group agree on a sequence despite some node failures.
06.06.design: It needs a quorum and has a latency cost; place it around metadata or critical state, not every cache hit.
06.06.mechanics: Consensus protocols such as Raft or Paxos elect a leader and replicate an ordered log after a quorum agrees. Safety means nodes do not commit conflicting entries; liveness depends on timing and quorum availability.
06.06.example: A cluster can use consensus to choose the owner of a partition or commit configuration changes. A write is considered committed only after the protocol’s required replicas acknowledge it.
06.06.failure: A quorum loss prevents new commits even if some nodes are healthy. Network delays can trigger leader changes and retries, so consensus is inappropriate for every high-volume request path.
06.06.review: What state truly requires one ordered decision, and which quorum failures should stop writes rather than permit conflicting progress?

06.07.thesis: Leader election gives one node authority to coordinate a task for a term.
06.07.design: Use a term or epoch on its writes so an old leader cannot continue acting after losing leadership.
06.07.mechanics: Leader election selects a coordinator for a term or epoch. A lease can reduce unnecessary overlap, but an old leader may keep running after it loses the right to lead.
06.07.example: A Raft-style election increments a term, obtains votes, and rejects messages from older terms. Workers receiving a new term can stop accepting stale assignments.
06.07.failure: A paused or partitioned previous leader can resume and write using old authority. Fencing at the protected resource is needed when stale writes would corrupt state.
06.07.review: Where is the elected term checked on every protected mutation, and can a former leader’s delayed request still be accepted?

06.08.thesis: A lease expires if not renewed, allowing another worker to take ownership.
06.08.design: Protect the resource with a fencing token; a paused worker may resume after its lease has expired.
06.08.mechanics: A distributed lock grants temporary ownership across processes, while a lease lets ownership expire unless renewed. Neither can stop a paused process from waking after expiry.
06.08.example: A scheduler can lease a job for 30 seconds and renew while processing. Store the lease owner and expiry atomically; if renewal fails, the worker stops and does not publish results.
06.08.failure: Clock differences and long pauses create overlapping beliefs about ownership. A lock service may grant a new lease while an old process still holds an open socket to the resource.
06.08.review: Can the resource reject operations from an expired owner, and what is the maximum lease/renewal uncertainty?

06.09.thesis: A Redis lock can reduce overlap, but lock ownership alone cannot stop a delayed former owner.
06.09.design: Pass increasing fencing tokens to the protected storage system and reject stale tokens there.
06.09.mechanics: Redis locks can coordinate best-effort exclusive work, but a lock’s random token only protects safe release. Fencing tokens add a monotonically increasing order that the protected resource enforces.
06.09.example: Acquire a lock with a unique token and expiry; release only if the stored token still matches. For a durable storage write, attach an increasing fencing number and reject any number lower than the latest accepted.
06.09.failure: A client can pause past lock expiry, another client can acquire it, then the first resumes and writes. The Redis lease alone cannot prevent that stale write.
06.09.review: Does the downstream database compare fencing tokens atomically, and how is token order preserved across lock-service restart?

06.10.thesis: Circuit breakers stop repeated calls to an unhealthy dependency and probe for recovery later.
06.10.design: Pair them with bounded timeouts and fallback behavior; an open breaker should fail quickly and visibly.
06.10.mechanics: A timeout bounds resource use; a circuit breaker tracks recent failures and temporarily stops calls; a bulkhead isolates pools so one dependency cannot consume all capacity.
06.10.example: A recommendation service can give the search dependency a short deadline, a small dedicated connection pool, and a fallback to cached suggestions. The breaker probes recovery after a cool-down.
06.10.failure: A breaker with a shared threshold may trip because of a local burst or stay open after recovery. Retrying beneath the breaker can still flood the dependency, and fallback may have its own limits.
06.10.review: Are deadlines budgeted end to end, and are dependency pools isolated so one slow service cannot occupy all request slots?

06.11.thesis: Gossip spreads membership or state through periodic peer exchange without a central broadcaster.
06.11.design: Convergence takes time, so do not use gossip as the only source of immediate truth for a critical decision.
06.11.mechanics: Gossip exchanges membership or state among peers in small rounds, allowing information to spread without a central broadcaster. Convergence is gradual and probabilistic.
06.11.example: Each node periodically tells a few peers its membership version and recent health observations. Rumor-mongering spreads updates across the cluster without every node contacting every other node.
06.11.failure: A node may be falsely suspected during a network delay, and inconsistent views persist until enough exchanges occur. Critical ownership changes still need stronger agreement than gossip alone.
06.11.review: Which information can converge eventually, and what mechanism resolves conflicting or safety-critical ownership claims?

06.12.thesis: A metadata service maps partitions and services to current owners.
06.12.design: Version the map and handle stale clients during movement; discovery itself needs a reliable bootstrap path.
06.12.mechanics: A metadata service stores cluster maps, shard ownership, schema versions, or service discovery records. Clients use it to find the current destination for work.
06.12.example: A partition map can associate shard ranges with replica sets and carry an epoch. Clients cache it briefly, route by epoch, and refresh when a server rejects an outdated map.
06.12.failure: Stale metadata can direct writes to a former owner during migration. If discovery itself has one unreplicated source, the cluster may be alive but unable to bootstrap.
06.12.review: How do clients detect stale maps, and what durable control plane remains available during a coordinator failure?

06.13.thesis: A distributed hash table locates keys through peer routing rather than one central index.
06.13.design: Account for churn, replication, and routing hops; the theoretical lookup cost is only part of operational latency.
06.13.mechanics: A distributed hash table routes a key through peer membership to a responsible node, commonly reducing hop count as the network grows. Replication and maintenance handle churn.
06.13.example: A peer can use a routing table to forward a lookup toward the node whose identifier is closest to a key. Successive peers narrow the distance without a central directory.
06.13.failure: Peer joins, departures, and partitions make routing tables stale. Replicas can disagree, and untrusted peers may return missing or manipulated values.
06.13.review: What consistency and integrity checks validate a result, and how quickly can routing recover after a peer disappears?

07.01.thesis: A storage engine must balance latency, throughput, durability, write amplification, and device behavior.
07.01.design: List read and write shapes first; the best layout for random point reads differs from one for sequential ingest.
07.01.mechanics: Storage engine design starts with operation mix, value size, durability target, device profile, and read/write amplification. The engine chooses what to keep in memory and how to lay bytes on disk.
07.01.example: For a write-heavy key-value workload, append records sequentially and keep a compact index in memory. For a small dataset with frequent range scans, sorted pages may give better reads.
07.01.failure: Foreground speed can conceal background compaction cost and temporary disk requirements. Ignoring fsync behavior or device failure makes the durability story incomplete.
07.01.review: What are the dominant operations, and what disk and memory work does each accepted write create over its full lifetime?

07.02.thesis: In-place updates favor some reads; append-oriented designs favor writes and later pay for compaction.
07.02.design: Measure total I/O, not only foreground latency, because maintenance competes with serving traffic.
07.02.mechanics: Storage engines trade write amplification, read amplification, space amplification, and recovery time. Optimizing one commonly increases another.
07.02.example: An LSM engine turns random updates into sequential writes, then reads may consult several levels. A B-tree updates pages in place, but random writes can cause page and log traffic.
07.02.failure: Benchmarks with a warm cache or no compaction misrepresent production behavior. Compare steady state, recovery, and peak maintenance in addition to isolated request latency.
07.02.review: Which amplification matters most for this workload, and what happens when compaction or checkpointing falls behind?

07.03.thesis: A file-backed dictionary can append key-value records and rebuild an in-memory offset index on startup.
07.03.design: Define framing, deletion markers, and crash recovery before treating the file as durable storage.
07.03.mechanics: A file-backed dictionary can append key/value records and store the latest file offset for each key in an in-memory hash map. Deletes need tombstones; startup reconstructs the map by scanning.
07.03.example: On process start, scan each record’s length, key, and value, keeping the offset for the newest occurrence. A lookup seeks to that offset; compaction copies only live values into a new file.
07.03.failure: A crash during a partial record must not make later bytes unparsable. A giant in-memory key index limits data size, and a torn compaction swap can lose the active file.
07.03.review: How are records framed and checksummed, and how does startup distinguish a valid last record from a torn write?

07.04.thesis: A binary format needs a versioned header, length fields, checksums, and an unambiguous byte order.
07.04.design: Reject truncated or corrupt records safely; leave room for readers that lag a writer version.
07.04.mechanics: A binary file format needs an explicit header, version, record boundaries, byte order, lengths, and integrity checks. Readers should reject malformed lengths before allocation.
07.04.example: A record might encode a magic value, version, key length, payload length, key, payload, and checksum. The parser checks declared sizes against file bounds before reading the body.
07.04.failure: An unchecked length field can trigger huge allocations or read beyond the file. Without versioning, one change in encoding can make all stored records unreadable.
07.04.review: Can an old reader safely reject a newer file, and can every record be located and verified without trusting its own length blindly?

07.05.thesis: Byte-range requests read a selected segment of a large object without transferring the whole file.
07.05.design: Keep an index of offsets and lengths, and make object versions immutable so offsets remain valid.
07.05.mechanics: Byte-range indexed object storage maps logical records to byte offsets in larger immutable objects. Range reads reduce transfer when a caller needs only one segment.
07.05.example: Write a sorted index of keys, offsets, and lengths alongside a packed data object. A request finds the index entry and fetches only the corresponding byte range from object storage.
07.05.failure: If object contents are overwritten, old offsets point to different data. Index and object versions must be published together; many tiny range requests can also cost more than one full download.
07.05.review: Are offsets tied to an immutable object version, and when is reading the whole object cheaper than issuing ranges?

07.06.thesis: Immutable data files let readers hold an old version while writers publish a new one atomically.
07.06.design: Use a manifest or pointer swap, then collect old versions only after readers no longer need them.
07.06.mechanics: Immutable versioned files are published by writing a complete new object and atomically changing a manifest or pointer. Readers can keep using the version they opened.
07.06.example: Build a new sorted snapshot in a temporary key, validate its checksum, then update the manifest to reference it. Keep the old version until no reader or rollback needs it.
07.06.failure: Replacing a file in place can expose partial content to readers. Old versions accumulate without lifecycle cleanup, and metadata publication can get ahead of durable data.
07.06.review: What operation makes a version visible atomically, and how long must previous versions remain available?

07.07.thesis: A log-structured store appends new records and resolves the latest value through an index or merge.
07.07.design: Compaction reclaims superseded data, but consumes disk and I/O that must be budgeted.
07.07.mechanics: Log-structured storage appends changes and resolves the newest value through an index, with compaction eventually rewriting live records. Sequential writes can improve throughput on many devices.
07.07.example: Write an update at the log tail and point the in-memory index to its offset. A later merge creates a clean segment with only the newest values and valid tombstones.
07.07.failure: A slow merge increases read amplification and disk use; deleting an old value too early can resurrect it from an uncompacted segment. Recovery scans need bounded checkpointing.
07.07.review: How does compaction prove that an older value or delete marker is safe to discard across all segments?

07.08.thesis: Bitcask writes values to an append-only log and keeps key-to-offset pointers in memory.
07.08.design: It offers simple fast point lookups when keys fit in memory; segment merge and crash rebuild need care.
07.08.mechanics: Bitcask combines append-only data segments with an in-memory key-to-file-offset index. It favors fast point lookups when the key index fits in RAM.
07.08.example: For each put, append a record and update the index. On restart, scan segment files in order; merge old segments by retaining only the latest value per key.
07.08.failure: A large keyspace can exceed memory, while a crash between log append and index update requires rebuild. Merge must preserve deletes and avoid removing a value still referenced by a reader.
07.08.review: What is the expected index memory per key, and what is the restart and merge duration at the largest supported dataset?

07.09.thesis: An LSM tree writes into memory, flushes sorted files, and compacts overlapping files later.
07.09.design: It trades fast sequential writes for read and compaction amplification; tune for the actual workload.
07.09.mechanics: An LSM tree writes into a mutable memtable, flushes sorted runs, and compacts overlapping levels. Writes are mostly sequential; reads may inspect multiple levels.
07.09.example: A key lookup checks the active memtable and immutable memtables, then uses Bloom filters and indexes to inspect sorted tables newest-first. Tombstones mask older versions until compaction removes them.
07.09.failure: If compaction cannot keep up, disk usage and read latency grow. Level sizing, write stalls, and extra free disk for compaction must be planned as operational limits.
07.09.review: At peak ingest, can background compaction process bytes faster than new data accumulates?

07.10.thesis: A memtable holds current writes, a WAL protects them, and SSTables store sorted durable runs.
07.10.design: Recovery replays the WAL after the last durable flush; flush and log truncation must be coordinated.
07.10.mechanics: The WAL preserves writes before a memtable is flushed; the memtable provides fast current lookups; SSTables are immutable sorted files. Their boundaries define recovery correctness.
07.10.example: Append and fsync a WAL record, apply it to the memtable, then acknowledge the write. When the memtable reaches a threshold, flush to an SSTable and only then retire the covered log segment.
07.10.failure: Deleting the WAL before the SSTable is durable loses acknowledged data. A flush failure or manifest mismatch can leave files on disk that recovery does not know about.
07.10.review: Which exact fsync and manifest steps must complete before a log segment can be deleted safely?

07.11.thesis: Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain a key; sparse indexes locate a nearby block within a sorted file.
