07.11.design: False positives still require reads, and checksums should cover blocks returned from disk.
07.11.mechanics: An LSM read checks memory, then uses per-file Bloom filters to rule out misses and sparse indexes to locate candidate blocks. Newer levels take precedence for overwritten keys.
07.11.example: For key K, skip each SSTable whose filter says absent; for possible matches, binary-search its sparse index and read one block. Compare versions and stop once a newer value or tombstone is authoritative.
07.11.failure: False positives increase I/O but must not create wrong answers. A corrupt filter can cause false negatives and hide data, so filters require checksums or safe rebuild behavior.
07.11.review: Can the read path recover from a missing filter by checking the file, and how many disk blocks does a typical point lookup touch?

07.12.thesis: Compaction merges sorted runs and discards overwritten or expired entries.
07.12.design: Track write amplification, temporary disk space, and stalls when compaction falls behind.
07.12.mechanics: Compaction merges sorted files, removes superseded versions, and reclaims tombstoned data. Write amplification is the total bytes rewritten per logical byte ingested.
07.12.example: A leveled compaction may rewrite a record through several levels to keep read fanout low; a tiered strategy merges less often but lets more overlapping files accumulate.
07.12.failure: Compaction can fill the disk with temporary output or monopolize I/O. Tombstones cannot be dropped until all older copies are known to be compacted.
07.12.review: What free-space reserve is required for the largest merge, and can foreground writes continue if compaction throttles?

07.13.thesis: Object storage stores large blobs cheaply and durably; databases provide indexed records and transactions.
07.13.design: Keep blob bytes and searchable metadata in separate systems with a clear consistency workflow.
07.13.mechanics: Object storage addresses large immutable blobs by key and offers durable bulk access; databases provide indexed records, transactions, and queryable fields. They often work together.
07.13.example: Store a photo blob in object storage and keep owner, dimensions, visibility, and object version in a relational row. A metadata lookup authorizes the request before a signed download URL is issued.
07.13.failure: Writing the row and blob is not one transaction. An uploaded object can become orphaned or a row can point to a missing object, so completion and cleanup workflows are required.
07.13.review: Which system owns visibility and metadata, and how do you reconcile partial success between object upload and database commit?

07.14.thesis: An object store needs a metadata index, data placement, replication or erasure coding, and a read path that locates chunks.
07.14.design: Define how PUT becomes visible and how lost nodes are repaired without losing accepted objects.
07.14.mechanics: An S3-style service combines metadata lookup, multipart data transfer, placement, checksums, replication or erasure coding, and lifecycle policy. The public API hides a distributed storage fleet.
07.14.example: A PUT can write chunks to independent nodes, verify checksums and required durability, then publish one metadata record making the object visible. GET resolves the object version and streams verified chunks.
07.14.failure: A metadata record pointing to incomplete data violates read correctness; orphaned chunks consume space. Repair and version deletion must coordinate with concurrent reads.
07.14.review: What is the visibility commit point, and which independent copies or fragments must exist before the service acknowledges PUT?

07.15.thesis: Range partitioning preserves ordered scans but risks hot ranges; hash placement spreads keys but disrupts locality.
07.15.design: Choose according to dominant queries and plan how ownership changes as capacity grows.
07.15.mechanics: Range partitioning preserves key order and supports range scans but can place a sequential workload on one owner. Hash partitioning spreads keys but scatters nearby ranges.
07.15.example: Partition time-series events by tenant and time when queries scan recent tenant history, while splitting extremely active tenants into subranges or buckets. Hash a lookup key when balanced point reads dominate.
07.15.failure: Range boundaries become hotspots as keys arrive monotonically. Hashing makes range queries fan out across nodes and can make global order expensive.
07.15.review: Which query locality is more valuable, and how do you split a range that becomes hot without stopping writes?

07.16.thesis: A partition manager records which node owns each partition and coordinates moves.
07.16.design: Publish map versions atomically and let old owners redirect or reject stale requests during handoff.
07.16.mechanics: A partition manager tracks partition ownership and orchestrates copy, catch-up, and cutover. The map is versioned so clients and servers can reject stale routes.
07.16.example: Move shard 42 by copying a snapshot, replaying changes, briefly fencing writes or forwarding them, then publishing a new map epoch. Keep the old owner able to redirect requests during propagation.
07.16.failure: Changing the map before data catches up loses writes; accepting writes on both owners creates divergent state. A failed migration needs a reversible state machine and observable progress.
07.16.review: At each migration phase, which node accepts writes, and how are writes during copy replayed exactly once or safely deduplicated?

07.17.thesis: Object metadata maps names to versions, locations, sizes, and lifecycle state.
07.17.design: Make metadata durable and scalable; intact blobs are useless if their locating records disappear.
07.17.mechanics: An object metadata database maps a logical name and version to size, checksums, lifecycle state, and physical placement. It is the index that makes opaque blobs discoverable.
07.17.example: A GET first resolves `(bucket, key, version)` to a manifest of chunks and locations, checks authorization, then retrieves the needed data. A list operation uses a separately indexed prefix path.
07.17.failure: Losing metadata can make intact object bytes unreachable. Listing and version deletion can race with upload completion unless the metadata state machine is explicit.
07.17.review: Can metadata be rebuilt from storage, and what consistency does a LIST promise while objects are being created or deleted?

07.18.thesis: An append-only stream assigns each record a stable position and advances readers with offsets.
07.18.design: Retention, segment rolling, and consumer lag determine when old data can be removed.
07.18.mechanics: An append-only stream stores records at stable offsets in ordered partitions. Consumers maintain their own checkpoints, allowing replay and independent processing.
07.18.example: A producer appends order events to partitioned logs. Analytics and fulfillment each read from their own offset; retention removes segments only after the replay window expires.
07.18.failure: Slow consumers may fall behind retention and lose the ability to replay. Partition count fixes parallelism and ordering scope, while one hot key can saturate a partition.
07.18.review: How long must a consumer be able to recover, and what happens when its committed offset is older than retained data?

07.19.thesis: Durability requires accepted writes to survive the chosen failure set, such as one disk or one availability zone.
07.19.design: Count only acknowledgements from independent failure domains and test recovery from a lost replica.
07.19.mechanics: Durability depends on independent copies, acknowledgement policy, repair, and tested restoration. Replication protects against selected node failures; backups protect against logical deletion and broader corruption.
07.19.example: Require writes to reach replicas in separate fault domains before acknowledging. Run anti-entropy checks and replace a failed replica while retaining enough healthy copies to serve traffic.
07.19.failure: Three replicas in one rack share a power failure, and replication copies accidental deletion immediately. Backups need separate credentials and restore tests to cover those cases.
07.19.review: Which failures are covered by replicas, which need backups, and what is the measured restore point and restore duration?

07.20.thesis: Checksums detect corruption across memory, network, disk, and later reads.
07.20.design: Verify at each handoff and retain an independent good copy so detection can lead to repair.
07.20.mechanics: Checksums detect accidental corruption by hashing data at write, transfer, and read boundaries. End-to-end verification ensures the bytes received match what the producer intended.
07.20.example: Store a checksum in object metadata, verify each chunk after upload and again after download, and use a known-good replica to repair a mismatch. Include checksum algorithm and scope in the manifest.
07.20.failure: A checksum detects damage but cannot recover bytes without another valid copy. Recomputing only at the destination can miss corruption that occurred before the checksum was recorded.
07.20.review: Where is the expected checksum created and durably stored, and what healthy source repairs a failed verification?

08.01.thesis: Move work off a request path when the user does not need its result before receiving a response.
08.01.design: Persist the task before acknowledging it, and expose completion or failure through a status record.
08.01.mechanics: Delegation moves nonessential work out of the synchronous request path. The handoff must be durable before the caller is told the work has been accepted.
08.01.example: An image upload endpoint can validate metadata, save an upload record, enqueue a thumbnail job, and return a job ID. A worker later creates variants and updates the record to ready or failed.
08.01.failure: If the process returns success before writing the task, a crash loses user work. If a worker retries after producing output, side effects can duplicate unless outputs are versioned or idempotent.
08.01.review: What durable state proves acceptance, and how can the caller discover completion or retry a failed job?

08.02.thesis: A task queue gives one worker a job; an event stream lets several consumer groups read the same ordered history.
08.02.design: Choose based on delivery and replay needs, then make each handler safe for repeated delivery.
08.02.mechanics: A task queue represents work to be claimed and completed, usually removing or acknowledging it after success. An event stream retains ordered records for multiple consumers and replay.
08.02.example: Send an email task to one worker pool; publish `OrderPlaced` to a stream that billing, analytics, and notification consumers each read independently.
08.02.failure: Using a queue for facts that multiple teams need can make fanout awkward. Treating a stream as a work queue without tracking consumer lag can repeat old work indefinitely.
08.02.review: Should one worker own this task, or should independent consumers replay the same event history?

08.03.thesis: A product event bus decouples producers from notifications, analytics, and other readers.
08.03.design: Publish an event only after the underlying state change is durable, often through an outbox.
08.03.mechanics: An event bus routes facts from producers to interested consumers. The producer should commit business state and event intent together, while consumers process at least once and deduplicate.
08.03.example: Write an order and an outbox event in one database transaction. A relay publishes the event, marks it sent, and retries after a broker outage; each consumer records processed event IDs.
08.03.failure: A direct dual write can commit the order but fail to publish, or publish an event for a rolled-back order. Duplicate publication is normal and must not double-charge or double-notify.
08.03.review: What makes the event publication atomic with the business change, and how does each consumer handle duplicates?

08.04.thesis: Queue lag is the age or count of work waiting for processing.
08.04.design: Alert on the oldest item and estimate catch-up time; worker count alone does not reveal whether users are falling behind.
08.04.mechanics: Queue lag measures work waiting, often by age of oldest message or distance between produced and consumed offsets. Throughput and lag together show whether processing capacity matches arrivals.
08.04.example: If producers add 500 jobs per second and workers finish 450, the backlog grows by 50 per second. Estimate drain time from queued work and spare throughput, not just worker count.
08.04.failure: A queue can have many recently added jobs but low user impact, or one old job blocking a critical workflow. Retries and poison messages can make a flat depth metric misleading.
08.04.review: What age of work violates the product promise, and can you estimate catch-up time during an alert?

08.05.thesis: A scheduler decides when a job becomes eligible, while workers perform it.
08.05.design: Use durable schedules and a lease or claim protocol so crashes do not silently lose jobs.
08.05.mechanics: A distributed scheduler stores schedules durably, determines eligible jobs, and claims work with leases so multiple scheduler nodes can cooperate.
08.05.example: Store each scheduled occurrence with a unique `(schedule_id, occurrence_time)` key. A scheduler claims due rows, enqueues them, and records the claim so a restart can resume safely.
08.05.failure: Wall-clock changes and scheduler downtime can skip or duplicate occurrences. Catch-up bursts after downtime may overload workers unless missed jobs have an explicit coalescing policy.
08.05.review: Are missed occurrences replayed, skipped, or coalesced, and what unique key prevents duplicate dispatch?

08.06.thesis: Workers can claim rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and process independent jobs concurrently.
08.06.design: Use a lease or retry state for crashed workers, and keep the claiming transaction short.
08.06.mechanics: PostgreSQL can act as a modest work queue by selecting eligible rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, claiming them in a transaction, and processing outside the lock.
08.06.example: Workers repeatedly claim a small batch, set a lease owner and expiry, commit, then handle jobs. Failed leases return to ready after expiry; completed jobs are marked or archived.
08.06.failure: Holding row locks during slow external work blocks vacuum and other workers. A worker crash after the external side effect but before marking complete can repeat the effect.
08.06.review: How are abandoned claims recovered, and is the external action idempotent across the commit gap?

08.07.thesis: A DAG workflow runs tasks after their dependencies complete.
08.07.design: Persist each step’s state and outputs so a restart can resume without repeating unsafe side effects.
08.07.mechanics: A DAG workflow models task dependencies explicitly; a node runs when its prerequisites succeed. Durable state records inputs, outputs, attempts, and status for restart and inspection.
08.07.example: A video workflow can validate upload, scan for malware, transcode renditions, create a manifest, then publish. Independent thumbnails and captions may run in parallel after validation.
08.07.failure: A retry from the beginning can repeat already successful steps. Cycles deadlock scheduling, and a workflow marked complete before outputs are durable misleads callers.
08.07.review: Can the workflow resume at the failed node, and are step outputs and side effects safe to reuse after a retry?

08.08.thesis: A rule engine maps events and conditions to actions without embedding every policy in application code.
08.08.design: Version rules, record why a rule fired, and cap recursive triggers to prevent loops.
08.08.mechanics: A rule engine separates event conditions and actions from compiled application branches. It needs a versioned rule format, deterministic evaluation, and traceable decisions.
08.08.example: When an account crosses a defined spend threshold, a rule can create a review task. Log the rule version, inputs, matched condition, and action so support can explain the result.
08.08.failure: Rules that trigger one another can form loops, and order-dependent rules produce surprising outcomes. Unbounded user-authored expressions can consume CPU or access data they should not see.
08.08.review: Can operators explain why a rule fired, and what prevents cycles, unsafe expressions, and uncontrolled evaluation cost?

08.09.thesis: Fanout can happen on write, on read, or through a shared log consumed by many downstream services.
08.09.design: A large audience turns eager fanout into a burst; hybrid delivery keeps ordinary users fast without overwhelming the system.
08.09.mechanics: Fanout distributes one event to multiple recipients or consumers. Push-on-write is fast at read time but pays work when publishing; pull-on-read delays fanout but adds work to each read.
08.09.example: For a social feed, precompute inbox entries for ordinary accounts and merge popular publishers at read time. A broker partition can spread recipient delivery while preserving per-recipient ordering if needed.
08.09.failure: A celebrity post can create a huge write burst; a consumer outage can leave partial delivery. Track fanout progress and make per-recipient insertion idempotent.
08.09.review: How many recipients can one event create at peak, and can delivery resume from a checkpoint without duplicates?

08.10.thesis: A flash sale is a contention problem: many buyers compete for a small number of units.
08.10.design: Reserve inventory atomically, expire abandoned holds, and make payment completion idempotent.
08.10.mechanics: Flash-sale inventory is a scarce-resource reservation problem. A successful hold reduces available units atomically; expiration or payment failure releases them exactly once.
08.10.example: Use a conditional update `available = available - 1 WHERE available > 0`, create a reservation ID, and set a short expiry. Payment confirmation transitions the same reservation to sold.
08.10.failure: A cache counter can oversell if multiple writers update nonatomically. A hold that never expires strands inventory, while releasing after payment succeeded can sell the same unit twice.
08.10.review: Which durable state transition owns the unit, and how do timeout, payment retry, and cancellation race safely?

09.01.thesis: Search has an ingestion path that builds an index and a query path that retrieves and ranks candidates.
09.01.design: Define freshness, relevance, and latency separately; a good index is useless if updates arrive too late.
09.01.mechanics: An information retrieval system ingests and normalizes documents, builds indexes, retrieves candidates, ranks them, and presents results. Freshness and relevance have separate measurement paths.
09.01.example: For product search, index title, brand, category, and availability; parse a query into lexical terms and filters, retrieve a candidate set, rank it, then hydrate current price and stock.
09.01.failure: A stale index can return unavailable items, while a ranking model may look good offline but bury exact product IDs. The system must balance index freshness, query latency, and authoritative fields.
09.01.review: Which fields may be stale in search, and which must be checked against live authoritative data before display or purchase?

09.02.thesis: An inverted index maps each term to a posting list of document IDs, often with positions and frequencies.
09.02.design: Compression and skip pointers reduce I/O; updates require segment or posting maintenance.
09.02.mechanics: An inverted index maps each normalized term to documents containing it, with optional frequency and positional information. Posting lists can be compressed and intersected efficiently.
09.02.example: To find documents containing both “distributed” and “cache,” read the two term lists and intersect document IDs. Positions enable phrase matches; term frequency can inform ranking.
09.02.failure: Common terms create large lists and expensive intersections. Tokenization differences between indexing and querying cause silent misses; updates leave stale postings until a merge or delete is applied.
09.02.review: Do index-time and query-time analyzers produce the same tokens, and how are deletes reflected in every posting list?

09.03.thesis: Boolean retrieval intersects and unions postings; tiered search scans the most promising subset first.
09.03.design: Keep a fallback to broader tiers when the top tier has too few results.
09.03.mechanics: Boolean search combines term sets with AND, OR, and NOT. Tiered retrieval checks cheap high-quality candidates first, then expands if too few results are found.
09.03.example: A query requiring brand and category can intersect selective postings, then add broader fuzzy matches only if the first tier is sparse. Track which tier produced each result for ranking.
09.03.failure: A selective filter applied after retrieval can discard all top candidates. A tiered system that never expands returns too few items and appears broken for rare queries.
09.03.review: How are candidate tiers ordered, and what minimum result count triggers a wider search?

09.04.thesis: TF-IDF raises the weight of a term that is frequent in one document but uncommon across the corpus.
09.04.design: Normalize for document length; raw term counts reward long documents unfairly.
09.04.mechanics: TF-IDF gives weight to terms that occur often in a document but are rare across the corpus. It is a useful baseline, but does not understand meaning or intent.
09.04.example: A document containing “consensus” several times may rank above one mentioning it once, while a corpus-wide common term contributes little. Normalize document length so long pages do not win by volume alone.
09.04.failure: Rare misspellings can receive high weight, and a document stuffing a term can game frequency. TF-IDF does not automatically account for freshness, field importance, or user intent.
09.04.review: Which corpus statistics and field weights affect the score, and what query set tests whether the ranking is useful?

09.05.thesis: BM25 combines term frequency saturation, inverse document frequency, and length normalization.
09.05.design: Tune it on judged queries and evaluate the whole ranking pipeline, not only the formula.
09.05.mechanics: BM25 scores term matches using inverse document frequency, term-frequency saturation, and document-length normalization. Parameters control how quickly extra occurrences stop helping.
09.05.example: A title match can receive more weight than body text, while BM25 balances term frequency and page length. Tune parameters using human relevance judgments and compare ranking at fixed query latency.
09.05.failure: A mathematically plausible score can rank the wrong items due to poor analyzers, missing fields, or mislabeled evaluation data. Global parameters may perform unevenly across query types.
09.05.review: What relevance judgments are used for tuning, and how does quality vary for exact IDs, broad queries, and long-tail terms?

09.06.thesis: Stop words reduce noisy postings, while champion lists keep top candidate documents for common terms.
09.06.design: Over-aggressive pruning can remove meaningful exact matches; preserve a route to complete retrieval.
09.06.mechanics: Stop-word removal reduces postings for very common terms; champion lists keep a small set of strong candidates for common queries. Both are retrieval shortcuts that can remove relevant documents.
09.06.example: A search engine can ignore “the” in broad text search but preserve it inside an exact phrase query. For common terms, first score a curated high-quality subset, then expand when needed.
09.06.failure: Removing a term can change a quoted phrase or a name. A champion list that is too small misses useful matches and can overfavor documents that were popular in the past.
09.06.review: Which query modes require exact token preservation, and how does the system detect that its first candidate tier is insufficient?

09.07.thesis: A query pipeline normalizes text, detects language, corrects terms, expands intent, and builds candidate requests.
09.07.design: Keep original terms available so a correction does not silently replace a precise user query.
09.07.mechanics: Query understanding normalizes text, tokenizes, detects language, handles spelling, extracts entities and filters, and may expand synonyms. Each transformation should preserve the original query for fallback.
09.07.example: For “nearby coffee open now,” detect a place category and time filter, retain “coffee” as a lexical term, and use location context only when the user supplied or allowed it.
09.07.failure: Aggressive stemming or correction can alter product codes and names. Inferring location or intent invisibly can violate privacy or produce confidently wrong results.
09.07.review: Can users inspect or undo inferred filters and corrections, and do rare names bypass broad normalization?

09.08.thesis: Clicks and dwell signals can improve ranking, but position bias makes high-ranked results look better even when they are not.
09.08.design: Log exposure and compare against controlled experiments before treating feedback as relevance truth.
09.08.mechanics: Search feedback includes impressions, clicks, dwell, reformulations, and purchases. It helps ranking only when exposure and selection bias are modeled.
09.08.example: Record which candidates were shown and their positions, not only which result was clicked. Compare changes with randomized experiments or counterfactual evaluation to separate relevance from position bias.
09.08.failure: Clicks are not pure relevance labels: top results get more exposure, and accidental clicks occur. Optimizing only clicks can reward sensational or misleading results.
09.08.review: What exposure data is needed to interpret a click, and what guardrail prevents one engagement metric from degrading task success?

09.09.thesis: Offline search evaluation compares retrieved results with judged relevant items using precision, recall, NDCG, and related measures.
09.09.design: Pair it with online latency and behavior metrics; a relevance lift that slows every query may not help users.
09.09.mechanics: Precision measures how many returned results are relevant; recall measures how many relevant items were found. Ranking metrics such as NDCG account for graded relevance and position.
09.09.example: For support search, judge a representative set of queries and documents, calculate precision at the first few results, and inspect cases where a known correct answer is absent entirely.
09.09.failure: A single aggregate score can hide failures for languages, query classes, or fresh documents. Judgments become stale when the corpus or product intent changes.
09.09.review: Which query segments and result positions matter to users, and how often are relevance labels refreshed?

09.10.thesis: A database update and its search-index update are separate writes with a failure gap.
09.10.design: Use an outbox or change stream, track lag, and make indexing idempotent so retries converge.
09.10.mechanics: Index synchronization propagates authoritative updates to a derived search index. A change log or transactional outbox closes the gap between database commit and index update.
09.10.example: Commit a catalog change and outbox event in one transaction; an indexer consumes the event, applies an idempotent update by entity version, and records its checkpoint.
09.10.failure: A direct database-plus-search dual write can update one system and not the other. Out-of-order events can overwrite a newer document unless version numbers are checked.
09.10.review: How is lag measured, and can replaying events out of order ever replace a newer indexed version?

09.11.thesis: Shard an index by document or term to spread storage and query work.
09.11.design: A coordinating node must merge results; skewed shards and cross-shard ranking complicate latency.
09.11.mechanics: Index sharding divides documents or terms across nodes. Document sharding makes writes and document ownership clear; query coordination merges top-ranked candidates from shards.
09.11.example: A coordinator broadcasts a query to several document shards, asks each for its top candidates, then merges scores and fetches needed fields. Routing by tenant can reduce unnecessary fanout.
09.11.failure: One slow shard can hold up a global result, and local top-k lists may omit a globally competitive result if the candidate budget is too small. Uneven document sizes create skew.
09.11.review: How many shards must each query touch, and how does the coordinator handle a slow or partial shard response?

09.12.thesis: A crawler discovers URLs, fetches pages politely, canonicalizes content, and feeds an indexing pipeline.
09.12.design: Deduplicate, honor crawl policies, and schedule recrawls according to change frequency.
09.12.mechanics: A crawler discovers URLs, enforces robots and politeness rules, fetches content, canonicalizes duplicates, extracts links and fields, then schedules recrawls.
09.12.example: Maintain a frontier keyed by host with per-host delay and retry state. Fetch a page, compute a content hash, and queue only changed normalized content for indexing.
09.12.failure: Retry storms can overload one domain; URL traps can generate infinite crawl spaces. Duplicate content wastes fetch and index capacity, and incorrect canonicalization can hide distinct pages.
09.12.review: How are per-host rate limits and crawl traps enforced, and what evidence decides a page needs recrawling?

09.13.thesis: Vector retrieval finds semantic neighbors; lexical retrieval preserves exact terms, identifiers, and rare names.
09.13.design: Combine candidate sets and rerank, then measure relevance on queries where the methods disagree.
09.13.mechanics: Vector retrieval compares embedding representations to find semantically similar items; lexical search remains better for exact terms and identifiers. Hybrid search combines candidates and signals.
09.13.example: Retrieve nearest vectors for conceptual queries and postings for exact product names, then merge and rerank with availability and textual features. Evaluate queries where lexical and semantic results disagree.
09.13.failure: Embedding models can miss new jargon or encode unwanted bias. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes trade recall for speed, and embedding version changes require coordinated reindexing.
09.13.review: How is candidate recall measured, and can the index mix vector versions without changing ranking semantics?

09.14.thesis: Autocomplete retrieves likely completions for a prefix under a tight latency budget.
09.14.design: Precompute popular prefixes, filter unsafe or private suggestions, and update popularity without rebuilding everything.
09.14.mechanics: Autocomplete predicts useful completions from a prefix with strict latency and privacy constraints. It can use a trie, finite-state structure, or precomputed popular prefixes.
09.14.example: Normalize a typed prefix, fetch a small set of popular completions, filter by locale and permissions, then rank by frequency, recency, and context. Cache common prefixes at the edge.
09.14.failure: A popular suggestion can expose a private or unsafe query. Large prefix fanout and per-keystroke requests need debounce, cancellation, and bounded response sizes.
09.14.review: Which signals are safe to personalize, and can a stale in-flight response overwrite suggestions for a newer prefix?

09.15.thesis: Spell correction generates plausible edits and ranks them using frequency and context.
09.15.design: Offer the correction without erasing the original query, especially for names, codes, and technical terms.
09.15.mechanics: Spell correction generates candidate edits and ranks them using term frequency, edit distance, and context. The interface should preserve the original query and offer a recoverable suggestion.
09.15.example: For an unknown token, generate nearby terms from a dictionary, score candidates in the surrounding phrase, then show “search instead for” while keeping original results available.
09.15.failure: A correction can corrupt names, identifiers, and low-frequency domain terms. Automatically rewriting without showing the original makes errors hard to diagnose and can hide valid content.
09.15.review: Which queries should bypass correction, and how does the UI make the corrected and original paths clear?

09.16.thesis: Related searches are alternative intents derived from aggregate query behavior or semantic similarity.
09.16.design: Avoid echoing a single user’s private history; rank suggestions by usefulness and diversity.
09.16.mechanics: Related searches connect a query to alternative intents using co-occurrence, semantic similarity, or curated rules. Suggestions should be useful without exposing an individual’s history.
09.16.example: Aggregate query transitions over enough users, remove sensitive or rare terms, and rank suggestions by relevance and diversity. Fall back to category-level suggestions when a query has little history.
09.16.failure: Raw query logs can include personal information. Co-occurrence can reinforce spam or popularity loops, and related terms may imply sensitive attributes.
09.16.review: What minimum aggregation protects privacy, and how do you prevent suggestions from narrowing users into one popular path?

09.17.thesis: Recent searches are a user-scoped ordered history with deletion and retention controls.
09.17.design: Keep private queries out of shared caches and honor clear-history requests across devices.
09.17.mechanics: Recent-search history is user-scoped data with explicit retention and deletion behavior. It should support multi-device consistency without becoming a public suggestion source.
09.17.example: Store normalized query, timestamp, and optional filters under an account, show a bounded list, and let a user remove one item or clear all devices. Cache results only under that user’s identity.
09.17.failure: A shared cache key can expose one person’s history to another. Deleting from the UI while retaining a replica or analytics copy breaks the stated privacy promise.
09.17.review: Where is history replicated, how long is it kept, and what does “clear” remove from each system?

10.01.thesis: Large counters can shard increments by key and time, then merge partial sums for reads.
10.01.design: Specify whether the displayed count must be exact and how late or duplicate events are handled.
10.01.mechanics: Exact counting at scale can shard counters and aggregate them later. The architecture must define deduplication, event-time windows, and whether reads are exact or approximate.
10.01.example: Hash each event ID to a worker-local counter, periodically flush deltas, and combine them for a dashboard. A durable log lets the system rebuild totals after a counter loss.
10.01.failure: Concurrent increments can be lost with read-modify-write; retries can count twice. Global hot counters serialize unless updates are partitioned.
10.01.review: Does the metric count requests or unique events, and what error or delay is acceptable in the displayed total?

10.02.thesis: A view is a defined event, not merely a page request; retries and refreshes can inflate it.
10.02.design: Choose deduplication identity and window, then state whether bot and repeated views count.
10.02.mechanics: A view count needs a product definition: page load, player start, minimum watch duration, or unique viewer in a window. The event producer and aggregation pipeline must use the same definition.
10.02.example: Emit a view candidate when a player starts, then qualify it after a threshold such as a minimum watch time. Deduplicate by viewer, content, and window before updating totals.
10.02.failure: Client retries, reloads, bots, and prefetch can inflate counts. Waiting for qualification delays the metric; counting at request time may measure traffic rather than actual viewing.
10.02.review: What exact event qualifies as a view, and which repeated or automated events should be excluded?

10.03.thesis: An impression should reflect actual exposure, often with viewport and duration criteria.
10.03.design: Emit the event once per eligible display and keep the definition stable across clients.
10.03.mechanics: An impression measures exposure, not merely delivery. A client often needs to report visibility, viewport intersection, and minimum duration for the item to count.
10.03.example: When a card is at least half visible for a short threshold, emit one impression ID tied to session and item. Batch events but preserve the event’s exposure timestamp and placement.
10.03.failure: Counting every item returned by an API overstates what people saw. Client-side blockers or offline devices create gaps, so exact global totals may be impossible.
10.03.review: What exposure threshold makes an impression meaningful, and how are repeated displays within a session treated?

10.04.thesis: HyperLogLog estimates distinct values using compact registers derived from hash patterns.
10.04.design: Its error is statistical; use exact sets for low-cardinality or correctness-critical decisions.
10.04.mechanics: HyperLogLog estimates distinct cardinality using hashed values and a compact set of registers. Its standard error is roughly proportional to the inverse square root of register count.
10.04.example: Hash each visitor ID, update the register selected by leading hash bits, and combine register maxima across workers. A daily dashboard can estimate uniques without storing every identifier.
10.04.failure: Hash collisions and small-cardinality bias affect estimates; exact billing or access decisions must not rely on an approximate distinct count. Register parameters set memory and error tradeoff.
10.04.review: What relative error is acceptable for this dashboard, and is the metric ever used to make a per-user decision?

10.05.thesis: Mergeable sketches combine summaries from shards without moving every raw event.
10.05.design: Check that the merge operation preserves the metric’s meaning and expected error bound.
10.05.mechanics: A mergeable sketch summarizes data so shard summaries can be combined with an operation that preserves metric meaning. It enables distributed aggregation without moving raw events.
10.05.example: Each worker can maintain a local distinct-count or quantile sketch and publish snapshots. A central reducer merges them by time bucket, avoiding one global write per event.
10.05.failure: Merging incompatible algorithm versions or overlapping windows can double count. Not every summary operation is safely mergeable, and approximate error can compound.
10.05.review: What exact merge law applies, how are versions tracked, and do source windows overlap?

10.06.thesis: Time buckets turn an unbounded stream into bounded windows that can be added and expired.
10.06.design: Decide how late arrivals update old buckets and whether queries need event time or processing time.
10.06.mechanics: Time-window aggregation groups events by event time or processing time into fixed or sliding buckets. Watermarks indicate how long the system waits for late events before finalizing a window.
10.06.example: For hourly active users, update the current hour’s sketch and accept late events for a bounded grace period. Queries sum finalized buckets and treat the active bucket as provisional.
10.06.failure: Late or out-of-order events can make a finalized number wrong. Very small buckets increase state and query cost; processing-time windows can misattribute delayed events.
10.06.review: What lateness is expected, and should a dashboard revise old windows or freeze them after a deadline?

10.07.thesis: Raw events preserve the ability to rebuild metrics; aggregates make common queries cheap.
10.07.design: Retain raw data long enough for corrections and document the derivation version of each aggregate.
10.07.mechanics: Raw events are the evidence from which derived analytics can be recomputed; aggregates are faster to query but encode assumptions and a transformation version.
10.07.example: Keep immutable click events with event ID and timestamp, then build daily per-campaign counts. If bot filtering changes, replay retained raw events into a new aggregate version.
10.07.failure: Deleting raw data too early prevents correction; retaining it forever raises privacy and storage cost. A dashboard without lineage cannot explain changes after a pipeline deploy.
10.07.review: Which raw fields and retention window are sufficient to rebuild the metric, and how are derivation versions labeled?

10.08.thesis: A count-min sketch estimates event frequency with small memory and one-sided overcount error.
10.08.design: Use independent hashes and size it for desired error; confirm heavy candidates against exact counts when needed.
10.08.mechanics: A count-min sketch uses several hash-indexed counter rows and returns the minimum observed counter as an estimate. Collisions only overestimate frequency.
10.08.example: For each event key, increment one bucket in every row. To estimate frequency, read those buckets and take the smallest, which reduces the effect of unrelated keys colliding in all rows.
10.08.failure: A sketch cannot safely report an exact count; frequent updates can overflow fixed-width counters. Width controls error and depth controls failure probability.
10.08.review: How much overcount is tolerable, and what overflow or reset policy applies to long-running counters?

10.09.thesis: A top-k summary tracks likely heavy hitters without storing every key.
10.09.design: Merge summaries carefully and verify finalists if the product requires exact rankings.
10.09.mechanics: Top-k heavy-hitter algorithms identify frequent keys while keeping bounded state. Candidate tracking and approximate counts let a stream avoid retaining every unique key.
10.09.example: Maintain a space-saving table of likely most-viewed items, then query exact counters for the candidates before displaying a ranked list. Merge worker candidates periodically.
10.09.failure: A true heavy hitter can be missed if windows or merge policies discard it. Delayed updates create unstable rankings, and “top” needs a clear time window.
10.09.review: What window defines top-k, and how are candidate recall and rank stability measured against exact samples?

10.10.thesis: Reservoir sampling keeps an unbiased fixed-size sample from a stream of unknown length.
10.10.design: Use it for estimation or inspection, not for rare-event guarantees.
10.10.mechanics: Reservoir sampling maintains a uniform fixed-size sample from a stream whose length is unknown. Every item has equal probability of appearing after the stream ends.
10.10.example: Keep the first k records, then for the nth subsequent event choose a random index from 1 through n and replace a sample slot only when the index is within k.
10.10.failure: A biased random function or per-partition reservoirs with unequal weights distort the sample. Sampling does not guarantee rare categories will appear.
10.10.review: Is the sample meant to represent all events uniformly, or must it preserve rare groups through stratified sampling?

10.11.thesis: A t-digest stores centroids that approximate quantiles, especially near distribution tails.
10.11.design: Merge digests across workers and validate tail error against known samples.
10.11.mechanics: A t-digest groups values into weighted centroids, allowing compact approximate quantiles with stronger accuracy near distribution tails. Compression controls size and precision.
10.11.example: Each service instance maintains a local digest of request latency and merges digests into a minute-level service summary. Query p50, p95, and p99 from the merged distribution rather than averaging local percentiles.
10.11.failure: Merge order and compression can affect accuracy; quantiles are not additive. Combining digests from different time windows can produce a plausible but meaningless percentile.
10.11.review: Are the merged digests built from the same units and time interval, and has tail error been checked against raw samples?

10.12.thesis: Streaming percentile dashboards summarize latency distributions over time windows.
10.12.design: Keep units and aggregation windows consistent; averaging p99 values is not the p99 of all requests.
10.12.mechanics: Streaming percentile analytics needs distribution summaries, not the mean of already-computed percentiles. Windows and tags determine which requests belong in each distribution.
10.12.example: Record latency observations or a mergeable histogram by service and region, then compute p99 for each rolling window. Keep sample count beside the quantile so a tiny population is not overinterpreted.
10.12.failure: Averages of p99 values do not equal the p99 of combined requests. High-cardinality labels explode storage, while sampling can miss rare slow tails.
10.12.review: Are percentiles merged from distributions, and do the labels preserve enough context without creating unbounded cardinality?

10.13.thesis: Live reactions can absorb bursts in a queue or stream, aggregate briefly, and push compact updates to viewers.
10.13.design: Persist individual reactions if undo and exact counts matter; the live display may tolerate a small delay.
10.13.mechanics: Live reactions combine high-rate writes, deduplication, counts, and fanout to connected viewers. The displayed count can be approximate while the underlying reaction ledger remains authoritative.
10.13.example: Store one reaction row per `(user, item, kind)` with an upsert, publish deltas to a stream, and aggregate updates per room for WebSocket clients. A remove action changes the same logical row.
10.13.failure: Counting every retry inflates totals; sending every reaction to every viewer overloads hubs. A delayed aggregation can briefly disagree with durable reaction rows.
10.13.review: Which state is exact, which display can lag, and how does reconnecting a viewer reconcile to an authoritative snapshot?

11.01.thesis: WebSocket gateways hold many connections while a shared data layer tracks subscriptions and updates.
11.01.design: Partition by connection or topic, limit fanout, and reconnect clients with a cursor after a gateway restart.
11.01.mechanics: WebSocket scaling separates connection gateways from shared subscription and message state. Each gateway holds local sockets, while a broker or routing layer moves updates to the right gateway.
11.01.example: A client connects to one gateway, subscribes to a room, and receives broker events for that room. Store a resumable cursor so a reconnect can request missed messages.
11.01.failure: Gateway restart drops all local sockets at once. Without connection limits, heartbeats and idle clients consume file descriptors and memory; shared pub/sub can create a fanout hotspot.
11.01.review: How many connections and subscriptions fit per gateway, and how does a client recover events missed during reconnect?

11.02.thesis: WebSockets support bidirectional messages, SSE streams server events over HTTP, and long polling repeatedly waits for updates.
11.02.design: Choose by direction, browser support, infrastructure, and reconnect behavior.
11.02.mechanics: WebSockets provide full-duplex communication, SSE provides one-way server-to-client streaming over HTTP, and long polling repeatedly holds a request open. Their reconnect and proxy behavior differ.
11.02.example: Use SSE for a dashboard that receives updates but sends actions through ordinary HTTP. Use WebSockets for collaborative editing where clients exchange frequent bidirectional operations; long polling suits simpler fallback clients.
11.02.failure: WebSockets require connection lifecycle and heartbeat management; SSE can be buffered by intermediaries; polling adds repeated request overhead and update delay.
11.02.review: Does the client need to send messages over the same channel, and which network intermediaries must the connection survive?

11.03.thesis: Store users, posts, follows, and interactions around the queries the product actually needs.
11.03.design: Separate the authoritative relationship edge from cached counts and derived feed materializations.
11.03.mechanics: Social data models users, posts, follows, reactions, and visibility. The best schema follows common reads: user profile, post timeline, followers, and access checks.
11.03.example: Store canonical follow edges with a unique `(follower_id, followed_id)` key. Maintain separate indexes for incoming and outgoing edges if both follower lists and following lists are common.
11.03.failure: Denormalized feeds and counts can retain private or deleted content after policy changes. A “like count” should not be mistaken for an authoritative list of users who liked a post.
11.03.review: Which relationships are canonical, and what derived data must be invalidated when a user blocks, unfollows, or deletes content?

11.04.thesis: A follow graph is a directed edge set with high-degree celebrities and uneven query patterns.
11.04.design: Index both follower and following directions or keep dedicated views; account for hot nodes.
11.04.mechanics: A social graph is a directed, potentially high-degree edge set. Traversal direction, edge updates, and high-degree account behavior determine storage and cache shape.
11.04.example: To render “people you follow,” read outgoing edges; to fan out a new post, enumerate incoming followers. Cache a celebrity’s follower routing separately rather than placing every edge in one hot row.
11.04.failure: High-degree nodes overwhelm one partition and fanout workers. Stale edges after block or unfollow can expose content unless authorization is checked at delivery or read time.
11.04.review: Which graph traversals are required, and how are privacy changes enforced against already materialized feed entries?

11.05.thesis: Push feeds prefill inboxes, pull feeds assemble them at read time, and hybrid feeds choose per publisher or audience.
11.05.design: Celebrities make push expensive, while pull increases read latency; model both traffic shapes.
11.05.mechanics: Push feed generation writes a post into followers’ inboxes; pull assembles followed accounts at read time; hybrid approaches select based on audience size and activity.
11.05.example: Push from ordinary accounts when they publish, but pull posts from high-follower accounts when a user opens the feed. Merge candidates by timestamp or ranking score, then filter current visibility.
11.05.failure: Write fanout costs rise with follower count, while pull work rises with follow count and read frequency. Feed materialization can preserve posts that later become private.
11.05.review: What threshold selects push versus pull, and which authorization check remains authoritative at feed read time?

11.06.thesis: An unread badge compares the newest relevant item with the user’s last-seen position.
11.06.design: Store a monotonic cursor and define whether edits, deletions, and multiple devices change the badge.
11.06.mechanics: An unread indicator compares a user’s last-seen cursor with the newest eligible item. A monotonic position is usually safer than incrementing an approximate badge.
11.06.example: Store `last_seen_sequence` per user and conversation. When a new message arrives with a higher sequence, compute unread from messages after that cursor; update the cursor when the user views the thread.
11.06.failure: A counter can drift after duplicate events or cross-device updates. If read state uses client time, clock skew may mark unseen messages as read.
11.06.review: What stable ordering key defines “new,” and how are concurrent devices’ read cursors merged?

11.07.thesis: Extract hashtags using a clear tokenizer and keep a tag-to-content index.
11.07.design: Normalize case and Unicode consistently, and update the index when content changes or is removed.
11.07.mechanics: Hashtag extraction tokenizes content, normalizes tag spelling, and maintains a reverse index from tag to content. The parser must handle Unicode and punctuation consistently.
11.07.example: On post creation, parse hashtags, normalize case, and write edges `(tag, post_id)` in the same outbox-driven pipeline as search indexing. A post edit replaces old edges with the new set.
11.07.failure: Naive splitting breaks tags containing Unicode letters or underscores, and asynchronous cleanup leaves deleted posts in tag results. Unbounded tags can be abused for storage growth.
11.07.review: What normalization rules define the same tag, and how are edges updated on edit, delete, and moderation?

11.08.thesis: Model one reaction per user, target, and reaction type with a unique constraint.
11.08.design: Counts are derived and can lag; use idempotent writes and reconcile drift rather than trusting every increment.
11.08.mechanics: Reaction modeling stores the user’s chosen reaction as a unique relationship; counts are a derived aggregate. The data model should represent add, change, and remove explicitly.
11.08.example: Upsert by `(user_id, post_id)` with a reaction type. Publish an event after commit so counters can be updated asynchronously; periodically compare aggregates with the authoritative rows.
11.08.failure: A counter increment on every retry diverges from the unique reaction set. Changing reaction type needs decrement/increment semantics or recomputation, not a second independent row.
11.08.review: Can a retry add a second reaction, and how does a type change update counts atomically or repairably?

11.09.thesis: Photo tags need coordinates relative to the original image or a normalized coordinate space.
11.09.design: Transform them during crops and resizing, and enforce who may tag or remove a person.
11.09.mechanics: Photo-tag coordinates need a stable reference frame such as normalized coordinates from 0 to 1 relative to the original image. Cropping and rotation transform that frame.
11.09.example: Store `(x, y)` normalized against the canonical image plus the tagged user and creator. On a resized preview, multiply by the rendered dimensions; on crop, apply the crop transform before display.
11.09.failure: Pixel coordinates tied to one rendition drift across responsive layouts. Tags can reveal location or identity and need moderation, visibility, and removal controls.
11.09.review: Which image version defines the coordinates, and what permission checks apply when another viewer sees or edits the tag?

11.10.thesis: Live commentary is an ordered event stream delivered to many connected readers.
11.10.design: Use sequence numbers for reconnect and decide how late edits or corrections appear.
11.10.mechanics: Live commentary is an ordered stream of short events delivered to subscribers. It needs sequencing, moderation, replay, and an update policy for corrections.
11.10.example: Assign each event a monotonically increasing sequence per match, persist it, then publish to connected viewers. On reconnect, request all events after the last seen sequence.
11.10.failure: Socket delivery can duplicate or miss messages, and edits may arrive after later commentary. Without durable replay, a temporary disconnect creates permanent gaps.
11.10.review: What cursor detects a missed event, and how are deleted or corrected entries represented in a client’s ordered view?

12.01.thesis: Nearby search first narrows candidates with a spatial index, then computes accurate distance and ranks them.
12.01.design: Filter by availability and permissions before returning a close but unusable result.
12.01.mechanics: Nearby search uses a coarse spatial index to reduce the candidate set, then computes exact distance and applies product filters. The index resolution affects candidate count and boundary handling.
12.01.example: For a user location, query nearby grid cells, union candidate businesses, calculate geodesic distance, then filter by open status and category. Sort by distance or a blended relevance score.
12.01.failure: A single cell misses close points just across its edge. Location freshness, coordinate accuracy, and privacy can matter more than index speed.
12.01.review: Which adjacent cells are needed for the search radius, and how old may a stored location be?

12.02.thesis: Geohash turns nearby coordinates into common prefixes at a chosen resolution.
12.02.design: Query adjacent cells too; a close point may cross a cell boundary.
12.02.mechanics: Geohash interleaves latitude and longitude bits into a string whose common prefix identifies a rectangular cell. Longer prefixes mean smaller cells.
12.02.example: Choose a precision based on search radius, fetch the center prefix and neighboring prefixes, then deduplicate candidates and calculate exact distance.
12.02.failure: Cell width varies with latitude and prefix boundaries split nearby points. Prefix match is a candidate lookup, not proof that a point lies within the requested radius.
12.02.review: What precision bounds candidate volume at different latitudes, and how are neighboring cells enumerated?

12.03.thesis: H3 uses hexagonal cells, S2 uses hierarchical spherical cells, and geohash uses rectangular string prefixes.
12.03.design: Compare coverage, precision, and operational tooling for the actual geographic queries.
12.03.mechanics: H3 partitions the globe into hierarchical hexagonal cells; S2 uses a hierarchical sphere-covering based on cube projections; geohash uses rectangular cells encoded as prefixes.
12.03.example: Use cell IDs to group delivery drivers by region, query nearby cells, and refine to finer cells in dense cities. Convert coordinates through one tested library and version.
12.03.failure: Different grids have different boundary shape, resolution, and neighbor semantics. Mixing cell versions or assuming equal area can bias search near poles or borders.
12.03.review: Does the workload prioritize hierarchy, compact prefixes, or geometric uniformity, and how are cells versioned across services?

12.04.thesis: Redis GEO can keep a fast index of current positions for nearby candidate lookup.
12.04.design: Expire stale locations and persist authoritative state elsewhere if positions must survive cache loss.
12.04.mechanics: Redis GEO stores geospatial members and supports radius or box candidate lookups in memory. It can serve a low-latency hot path while durable location state remains elsewhere.
12.04.example: Update a driver’s current coordinates with an expiry timestamp, fetch nearby active drivers, then hydrate availability and eligibility from an authoritative service before dispatch.
12.04.failure: A stale member can match nearby even after a driver disconnects. Cache loss removes the index, and frequent moving updates can make a global hot region expensive.
12.04.review: How is stale position data expired, and what source confirms that a nearby candidate is actually available?

12.05.thesis: Geofencing tests whether a point falls inside a polygon, often after a bounding-box prefilter.
12.05.design: Define behavior at the boundary and use a consistent coordinate system.
12.05.mechanics: A geofence is a polygon or set of polygons with a coordinate reference system, boundary policy, and efficient candidate prefilter. Point inclusion is the final geometric test.
12.05.example: Index each fence by bounding box, find boxes that cover an incoming location, then test the point against candidate polygons. Emit an enter or exit only after comparing previous membership.
12.05.failure: GPS noise near a boundary can cause rapid enter/exit flapping. Invalid self-intersecting polygons or longitude wrap need validation before serving queries.
12.05.review: How are boundary points classified, and what hysteresis or accuracy threshold prevents GPS jitter from generating repeated transitions?

12.06.thesis: Ray casting counts intersections from a point to outside; odd counts mean inside.
12.06.design: Handle points on edges, vertices, and holes deliberately, because naive intersection rules disagree there.
12.06.mechanics: Ray casting draws a horizontal ray from a point and toggles inside/outside for each polygon-edge crossing. A consistent half-open edge rule avoids double-counting vertices.
12.06.example: For each edge, test whether it straddles the point’s latitude and whether the ray intersection lies to the right. Toggle a boolean for each valid crossing; odd means inside.
12.06.failure: A point exactly on an edge or vertex makes naive comparisons ambiguous. Floating-point precision and longitude wrap can create inconsistent results across implementations.
12.06.review: What is the exact boundary convention, and do all services use the same projected or geodesic coordinate assumptions?

12.07.thesis: A Bloom filter cheaply excludes definitely unseen items but may falsely mark a new item as seen.
12.07.design: Use an exact set when false exclusion is unacceptable, such as a paid entitlement.
12.07.mechanics: A Bloom filter is memory-efficient for likely-seen checks but can falsely report membership; an exact set uses more memory but has no false positives.
12.07.example: Use a Bloom filter to cheaply avoid querying a large seen-item store for most unseen candidates, then verify positives in an exact set when correctness matters.
12.07.failure: A false positive may hide a recommendation the user has never seen. Rebuilding the filter while writes continue can drop recent IDs unless updates are replayed.
12.07.review: What user-visible error follows a false positive, and which decisions still require exact membership verification?

12.08.thesis: Matching narrows eligible pairs, scores them, then applies capacity and fairness constraints.
12.08.design: Measure outcomes after assignment; the best local score may lead to poor global utilization.
12.08.mechanics: Matching creates eligible pairs, scores them, then assigns capacity while respecting constraints such as fairness, distance, and urgency. Recommendation ranking predicts relevance but must also enforce eligibility and diversity.
12.08.example: For ride dispatch, filter drivers by availability and pickup radius, score ETA and acceptance likelihood, then reserve the best candidate briefly. For recommendations, retrieve a diverse candidate set before ranking.
12.08.failure: Greedy local choices can leave global demand unmatched; feedback loops can overexpose already popular items. Eligibility changes between scoring and action require a final check.
12.08.review: What constraints are hard eligibility rules versus soft ranking signals, and how will outcome quality be measured across groups?

13.01.thesis: Give the client a short-lived scoped upload URL so file bytes go directly to object storage.
13.01.design: The application still validates ownership, content metadata, and completion before exposing the object.
13.01.mechanics: Direct uploads move large bytes from client to object storage while the application issues a narrow, short-lived capability. The server remains responsible for ownership and completion validation.
13.01.example: Create an upload row with owner and expected size, return a signed PUT URL for one object key, then verify checksum and object metadata before marking it available.
13.01.failure: A leaked URL can be used until expiry, and clients may upload unexpected content or enormous files. An object may arrive without a completed metadata record.
13.01.review: How narrowly is the signed permission scoped, and what verifies size, content type, checksum, and owner before publication?

13.02.thesis: An image CDN caches precomputed or on-demand resized variants near readers.
13.02.design: Bound allowed dimensions and formats, and include transformation parameters in cache keys.
13.02.mechanics: An image CDN caches source images and produces variants through fixed transformations. Cache keys must include every parameter that changes output.
13.02.example: Normalize allowed widths and formats, then generate URLs whose transformation set maps to a bounded cache key. Use a queue or edge transform for cold variants and cache them near readers.
13.02.failure: Arbitrary width and crop parameters allow cache-key explosion and expensive transforms. A stale variant may remain after a source image is removed or made private.
13.02.review: Which transforms are allowed, how many variants can one source create, and how does revocation invalidate cached copies?

13.03.thesis: An avatar service maps a user and image version to stable variant URLs.
13.03.design: Invalidate on change, provide a safe default, and avoid leaking private source images through public variants.
13.03.mechanics: An avatar service maintains a stable identity URL while mapping a user to a versioned source and responsive derivatives. Privacy policy determines whether those derivatives are public or signed.
13.03.example: Store a user’s avatar object version and generate small, medium, and high-density renditions. The profile API returns a stable path containing a version token so clients cache safely.
13.03.failure: Replacing an image without changing its cache version shows old avatars. Public CDN URLs can leak images after a profile becomes private unless access and purge behavior are explicit.
13.03.review: How does a change invalidate client and CDN caches, and can private avatars be fetched only by authorized viewers?

13.04.thesis: Multipart upload lets large videos resume parts rather than restarting from zero.
13.04.design: Scope signed URLs to one object and expiry, and verify completed parts and size before accepting metadata.
13.04.mechanics: Multipart upload divides a large object into independently retriable parts. The control plane creates an upload session and signed part URLs, then validates the final assembled object.
13.04.example: Create a multipart session, let the client upload numbered parts with checksums, persist returned part IDs, and call complete only after all expected parts are present. Abort abandoned sessions by lifecycle rule.
13.04.failure: A client may retry a part with different bytes or complete with a missing part. Incomplete uploads consume storage, and an expired URL should not invalidate a completed object.
13.04.review: How are part identity and checksum verified, and who cleans up abandoned multipart sessions?

13.05.thesis: A transcoding pipeline reads an uploaded source, produces renditions, packages segments, and publishes a manifest.
13.05.design: Treat each step as retryable and keep the source immutable until all required outputs are checked.
13.05.mechanics: Transcoding turns one source into multiple codecs, resolutions, and packaging formats. The pipeline is a state machine with retryable steps and an explicit publication point.
13.05.example: After upload, validate the source, probe metadata, enqueue renditions, verify each output, then publish a manifest. Track per-rendition status so a partial failure can resume only missing work.
13.05.failure: Publishing before all required renditions are verified exposes broken playback. Repeated jobs can waste compute unless outputs use deterministic keys and source versions.
13.05.review: What minimum rendition set is needed before publication, and how is a retry distinguished from a new source version?

13.06.thesis: Adaptive bitrate playback selects segments based on measured throughput and buffer health.
13.06.design: The CDN serves multiple renditions; the client’s switching policy trades picture quality against stalls.
13.06.mechanics: Adaptive bitrate playback switches among encoded renditions according to measured throughput, buffer health, and device capabilities. The CDN delivers segments; the player decides which representation to request.
13.06.example: A player begins at a conservative bitrate, estimates bandwidth from downloaded segments, and steps up only when the buffer can tolerate it. Segment manifests identify aligned time ranges across renditions.
13.06.failure: Abrupt quality changes or misaligned segments cause stalls. Throughput estimates lag sudden network changes, and CDN cache misses on uncommon renditions can increase startup time.
13.06.review: How does the player avoid oscillating between bitrates, and which segments remain aligned for a seamless switch?

13.07.thesis: Signed URLs limit access duration, while DRM manages licensed playback keys; neither replaces application authorization.
13.07.design: Check entitlement before issuing playback credentials and keep key delivery separate from public segments.
13.07.mechanics: Signed URLs grant time-limited access to a specific resource; DRM adds license and key control for protected media. Authorization, encryption, and client security are separate layers.
13.07.example: Verify the viewer’s entitlement, issue a short-lived manifest URL, and serve encrypted segments whose decryption key is returned through a license service. Log issuance without exposing key material.
13.07.failure: A signed URL can be copied during its validity; a long expiry weakens revocation. DRM does not stop screen capture or replace authorization at the application boundary.
13.07.review: What resource and time window does each token authorize, and how quickly can access be revoked after entitlement changes?

13.08.thesis: WebRTC prioritizes interactive low latency, while segmented live streaming scales to large audiences with more delay.
13.08.design: Choose the latency target first, then plan ingest, transcoding, distribution, and reconnect behavior.
13.08.mechanics: Live streaming architecture chooses an ingest protocol, transcode or package path, distribution method, and latency target. WebRTC supports interactive low delay; segmented delivery scales broadly with more buffering.
13.08.example: For a small interactive call, exchange WebRTC media through signaling and relay servers when NAT traversal fails. For a large event, ingest once, segment renditions, and distribute through a CDN.
13.08.failure: Low-latency paths cost more per viewer and are sensitive to jitter; large-scale segment delivery introduces delay. Capacity at ingest and egress must match the audience model.
13.08.review: What end-to-end latency is required, how many simultaneous viewers are expected, and what fallback applies when a relay or CDN path fails?

13.09.thesis: File sync compares local and remote versions, transfers changed data, and resolves concurrent edits.
13.09.design: Use version vectors or explicit conflict copies when both sides changed offline.
13.09.mechanics: Remote file sync compares manifests or versions, transfers changed blocks, and resolves concurrent edits. A durable operation log helps devices resume after disconnect.
13.09.example: Each device stores a base version and local changes. On reconnect, exchange version tokens, upload missing blocks, and create a new manifest; preserve a conflict copy if both sides changed the same file.
13.09.failure: A last-writer-wins timestamp can discard offline edits when clocks disagree. Deletion must propagate as a tombstone long enough for offline devices to learn about it.
13.09.review: How are concurrent updates detected, and how long are delete tombstones retained for devices that reconnect late?

13.10.thesis: Fixed-size chunks simplify addressing and retries; content hashes identify identical bytes for deduplication.
13.10.design: A small insertion shifts many fixed boundaries, so content-defined chunking may save more transfer on edited files.
13.10.mechanics: Chunking splits files for resumable transfer and deduplication; content addressing names chunks by a cryptographic digest. Fixed blocks are simple, while content-defined boundaries resist shift after inserts.
13.10.example: Hash each fixed-size block and upload only chunks absent from the server. A manifest records order and total file length; the receiver verifies hashes before assembly.
13.10.failure: A small insertion shifts every following fixed boundary, reducing deduplication. Hashes reveal equality across users and may expose whether a known sensitive file exists.
13.10.review: What chunking method fits the edit pattern, and how are cross-user deduplication and content-existence side channels controlled?

13.11.thesis: A file manifest lists chunk identities and order for one immutable version.
13.11.design: Publish a new manifest atomically, retain shared chunks while referenced, and garbage-collect unreferenced ones later.
13.11.mechanics: A blocklist or manifest maps a file version to an ordered set of chunk IDs. Immutable manifests make version publication atomic and let unchanged chunks be shared.
13.11.example: Upload changed chunks, create a new manifest referencing old and new chunk IDs, then switch the file’s current-version pointer. Garbage collection deletes chunks only when no retained manifest references them.
13.11.failure: Deleting a chunk based on one stale reference count can corrupt another version. Partial manifest writes or reordered updates can expose a file with missing blocks.
13.11.review: How are reference counts rebuilt or verified, and which manifest versions protect chunks from garbage collection?

14.01.thesis: Logs explain events, metrics show trends, and traces connect work across service boundaries.
14.01.design: Propagate correlation IDs and measure the user request from entry to response.
14.01.mechanics: Observability combines metrics for trends, structured logs for event details, and traces for causal paths across services. Correlation identifiers connect those views to one user operation.
14.01.example: Propagate a trace context from gateway to database and queue consumer. Record request IDs, outcome, and dependency duration while keeping high-cardinality values out of metric labels.
14.01.failure: A service can emit abundant logs but still lack the evidence needed to explain a slow request. Sensitive payloads in logs create privacy risk, and unbounded labels overwhelm the metrics backend.
14.01.review: Can an operator trace one failed user action end to end without storing secrets or creating unbounded metric series?

14.02.thesis: An SLO defines a target for a user-visible indicator; the error budget is the allowed misses in a window.
14.02.design: Use budget burn to guide release pace and incident priority, not as a substitute for understanding impact.
14.02.mechanics: An SLO targets a user-visible indicator over a fixed window; the error budget is the amount of failure the target permits. Burn rate says how quickly that budget is being spent.
14.02.example: If 99.9% of requests must succeed over 30 days, estimate the allowed failed-request count and alert on fast burn over shorter windows. Use the budget to prioritize reliability work and risky releases.
14.02.failure: A process-health target can remain green while user operations fail. A single monthly threshold may detect trouble too late, so fast and slow burn alerts complement each other.
14.02.review: Which user operation defines the indicator, and what short-window burn rate warrants paging rather than a ticket?

14.03.thesis: Incident response first stabilizes the service, then records a timeline and follows the evidence to causes.
14.03.design: Assign an incident lead and communicate status; review contributing conditions after recovery without blame.
14.03.mechanics: Incident response coordinates mitigation, investigation, and communication under time pressure. A timeline and clear roles reduce duplicate work and preserve facts for later learning.
14.03.example: Name an incident lead, an operations owner, and a communications owner. Stop the impact first with rollback or traffic shaping, record timestamps and hypotheses, then verify recovery using user-facing indicators.
14.03.failure: Uncoordinated responders can make conflicting changes and erase evidence. Declaring recovery from a green process check while requests still fail prolongs impact.
14.03.review: Who is coordinating, what metric proves mitigation, and where are decisions and timestamps recorded?

14.04.thesis: Safe releases use small batches, health gates, and a reversible switch to the prior version.
14.04.design: Ensure old and new versions coexist with current schemas and messages during rollout.
14.04.mechanics: Safe deployment uses small batches, health gates, progressive exposure, and a rollback or forward-fix plan. Application and schema changes must coexist during a rolling release.
14.04.example: Deploy to one canary, compare error and latency indicators with baseline, then increase traffic in stages. Keep the previous version compatible with any fields or messages written during rollout.
14.04.failure: A rollback may be impossible after a new version writes incompatible data. A canary without representative traffic or alert thresholds provides little safety.
14.04.review: What signal pauses rollout, and can the old version safely read data written by the new one?

14.05.thesis: Database migrations need compatible schema steps, controlled backfills, and verification of row counts or checksums.
14.05.design: Keep the old read path available until the new one proves correct under real traffic.
14.05.mechanics: Database migration safety combines compatible schema changes, throttled backfill, validation, cutover, and delayed cleanup. Large changes should be resumable and observable.
14.05.example: Add a new nullable column, deploy dual writes, backfill primary-key ranges with checkpoints, compare counts and hashes, switch reads, then stop old writes before dropping the old field.
14.05.failure: A single giant update can lock tables, fill logs, and trigger replication lag. Removing the old field too early breaks still-running code or rollback binaries.
14.05.review: Can the backfill resume after interruption, and what independent comparison proves the new representation matches the old?

14.06.thesis: A parallel monolith can receive a gradually increasing share of reads while the old system remains authoritative.
14.06.design: Compare responses, watch latency and errors, then move writes only after semantics are aligned.
14.06.mechanics: A parallel read drain sends a gradually increasing share of reads to a new implementation while the old path remains available for comparison. It reduces migration risk before writes move.
14.06.example: Mirror or shadow selected read requests to the new service without returning its result, compare normalized outputs, then serve a small percentage of live reads from it. Record diffs and latency.
14.06.failure: Shadow traffic can double backend load and may invoke side effects if handlers are not read-only. A low traffic sample may miss rare query shapes.
14.06.review: Can mirrored requests have side effects, and which representative segments must match before live reads switch?

14.07.thesis: A backup is useful only if a restore can produce consistent, usable data within the required time.
14.07.design: Test restores regularly and record the latest recoverable point, credentials, and dependencies.
14.07.mechanics: Backups capture recoverable state; restore tests prove that the backup, logs, keys, and runbook can rebuild a working service. Define recovery point and time targets.
14.07.example: Take periodic snapshots plus transaction logs, restore into an isolated environment, replay to a chosen time, and verify critical queries and checksums before measuring elapsed recovery.
